OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-Closure Glauc:
What & Why

Acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG) is a sight-threatening ophthalmic emergency in which the drainage angle of the anterior chamber becomes suddenly blocked, causing intraocular pressure (IOP) to rise rapidly + severely (often 50–80 mmHg vs normal 10–21). Delayed treatment — even by hours — causes irreversible optic nerve damage and permanent blindness; it presents as a classic red, painful eye with visual loss + nausea/vomiting.

The core mechanism: aqueous (made by the ciliary body) flows posterior chamber → through the pupil → anterior chamber → drains via the trabecular meshwork at the iridocorneal angle. In a susceptible eye (shallow anterior chamber, narrow angle), the iris bows forward and blocks the pupil (“pupillary block”) → aqueous can’t pass forward → pressure balloons the iris forward → it seals off the drainage angle → IOP shoots up. The trigger is often pupil dilation (mid-dilation is worst — the iris bunches into the angle).

Risk Factors
  • Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) — small eyes with shallow anterior chambers/narrow angles (the classic)
  • Increasing age (lens thickens/moves forward), female sex, Asian ethnicity, family history
  • Mydriasis-provoking triggers: dim light (cinema/dark room), pupil-dilating drugs — anticholinergics, tricyclic antidepressants, sympathomimetics, some antihistamines — and pharmacological dilation for fundoscopy (a classic exam trigger)
Presentation
📷 Image placeholder — Clinical photo of an acute painful red eye — a fixed, mid-dilated, oval, non-reactive pupil with a hazy/oedematous cornea
🩺 Symptoms
  • Sudden severe unilateral eye pain + headache
  • Blurred vision / reduced acuity, haloes around lights (corneal oedema)
  • Red eye; nausea + vomiting (vagal — may dominate + mislead)
  • The eye may feel hard (“like a marble”) on gentle palpation
🔍 On examination
  • Fixed, mid-dilated, oval, non-reactive pupil
  • Hazy/cloudy cornea (oedema) → reduced red reflex
  • Ciliary injection, shallow anterior chamber
  • Markedly raised IOP on tonometry (confirmatory)
Investigations
  • Tonometry — measure IOP (the key confirmatory test; often >40–50 mmHg)
  • Gonioscopy — visualises the closed drainage angle (definitive angle assessment)
  • Slit-lamp — corneal oedema, shallow anterior chamber, mid-dilated pupil
  • Assess the fellow eye (usually also narrow-angled → needs prophylactic treatment)
Management (RCOphth)
📷 Image placeholder — Emergency algorithm — lie flat + analgesia/antiemetic → IV/PO acetazolamide + topical beta-blocker/alpha-agonist/steroid ± mannitol → pilocarpine once IOP falls → definitive laser peripheral iridotomy to BOTH eyes
Emergency — immediate ophthalmology referral + start IOP-lowering treatment while awaiting them. Aim: rapidly lower IOP + relieve the pupillary block. Lie the patient flat, face up (lets the lens fall back); give analgesia + antiemetics.
💊 Medical IOP-lowering (started together)
  • IV/oral acetazolamide 500 mg (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) — ↓aqueous production; the single most useful systemic agent. Avoid in sulphonamide allergy + sickle cell
  • Topical beta-blocker (timolol) — ↓production (caution asthma/COPD/bradycardia)
  • Topical alpha-2 agonist (brimonidine/apraclonidine) — ↓production + ↑outflow
  • Topical steroid (prednisolone) — ↓inflammation
  • IV mannitol (osmotic) — if IOP not controlled
💧 Pilocarpine — timing matters
  • A miotic — constricts the pupil, pulling the iris away from the angle to reopen it
  • Only works once IOP is lowered — at very high IOP (>~40–50) the iris sphincter is ischaemic + pilocarpine is ineffective, so it’s given after IOP starts falling (defer if IOP >40)
Definitive treatment: laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) — a small hole in the peripheral iris creates an alternative channel for aqueous to bypass the pupillary block → equalises pressure → the iris falls back + the angle reopens. Performed in BOTH eyes (the fellow eye is predisposed → prophylaxis). Lens extraction (cataract surgery) is an increasingly used definitive alternative, especially with co-existing cataract.
Complications (if untreated/delayed)
  • Permanent visual loss / blindness (optic nerve infarction); optic atrophy
  • Central retinal artery or vein occlusion
  • Recurrent attacks; chronic angle-closure glaucoma
Exam Pearls
What it is
Ophthalmic EMERGENCY: sudden blockage of the drainage angle → rapidly rising IOP → optic nerve damage.
Triad
Red painful eye + reduced vision/haloes + nausea/vomiting.
Signs
FIXED, mid-dilated, oval, non-reactive pupil + hazy cornea + hard eye + very high IOP.
Mechanism
Pupillary block in a shallow anterior chamber / narrow angle (hypermetropes). Triggered by mydriasis (dark rooms, anticholinergics/TCAs, dilating drops).
Confirm
Tonometry (high IOP) + gonioscopy (closed angle).
Medical
Acetazolamide (IV/PO) + topical timolol + brimonidine + pilocarpine (once IOP down) + steroid ± mannitol.
Pilocarpine caveat
Doesn’t work at very high IOP (ischaemic iris) — use after IOP falls.
Definitive
Laser peripheral iridotomy — in BOTH eyes.
Don’t miss
Distinguish from open-angle (chronic, painless, gradual field loss). Dilated pupil + eye pain + vomiting can masquerade as migraine or acute abdomen.
OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related Macular Degen:
What & Why

Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is progressive degeneration of the macula — the central retina responsible for high-acuity central vision — and the leading cause of irreversible visual loss in older adults in the developed world. It robs central vision (reading, driving, faces) while sparing peripheral vision (so patients are rarely completely blind), and the wet form is a treatable emergency — prompt anti-VEGF preserves sight.

The core anatomy: the macula (with the fovea at its centre) has the highest cone density → central, detailed, colour vision. AMD damages the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), Bruch’s membrane + photoreceptors at the macula. Metabolic waste accumulates as drusen (yellow deposits) — the hallmark of AMD.

MechanismGradual RPE/photoreceptor atrophy + drusen; late = geographic atrophyChoroidal neovascularisation — abnormal vessels grow from the choroid through Bruch’s membrane; they leak/bleed

The key instinct: an elderly patient with sudden central visual distortion → suspect wet AMD → urgent referral (treatable window). Gradual bilateral central blurring over years → dry AMD.
Risk Factors
  • Increasing age (the dominant factor)
  • Smoking (the biggest modifiable risk — strongly linked)
  • Family history / genetics (complement factor H polymorphisms)
  • Caucasian ethnicity; hypertension, cardiovascular disease, poor diet (low antioxidants); female sex
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Amsler grid as the patient sees it — wavy distorted lines (metamorphopsia) with a missing central patch (scotoma); used at the bedside and for home self-monitoring
  • Gradual (dry) or sudden (wet) loss of central vision — difficulty reading, recognising faces
  • Metamorphopsia — straight lines appear wavy/distorted (classic, especially wet) — tested with an Amsler grid
  • Central scotoma (blank/dark central patch)
  • Reduced acuity, poor low-light adaptation, micropsia/macropsia (objects smaller/larger)
  • Peripheral vision preserved — reassurance + distinguishes from glaucoma
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — OCT — drusen/RPE change in dry AMD vs intra-/subretinal fluid signalling active wet AMD (the finding that guides anti-VEGF treatment)
  • Fundoscopy: dry — drusen (yellow macular deposits), RPE pigmentary changes, geographic atrophy (advanced); wet — macular haemorrhage, exudates, fluid/oedema, ± grey-green subretinal membrane
  • Amsler grid — reports distorted/missing lines (bedside + self-monitoring)
  • Optical coherence tomography (OCT) — the key investigation: cross-sectional retinal imaging showing fluid (intra-/subretinal), drusen + neovascular membranes; guides diagnosis + monitors treatment
  • Fluorescein angiography (FFA) — confirms + localises choroidal neovascularisation in wet AMD (shows leakage)
Management
🟡 Dry AMD
  • No cure to reverse it → supportive + slow progression
  • Smoking cessation (key modifiable factor)
  • AREDS2 supplements — high-dose antioxidants (vit C, E), zinc, copper, lutein, zeaxanthin — slow progression from intermediate to advanced (don’t reverse it or help early AMD)
  • Low-vision aids, sight-impaired registration; Amsler grid self-monitoring to catch conversion to wet
  • New: complement inhibitors (pegcetacoplan C3 / avacincaptad C5, intravitreal) — first treatments to slow geographic atrophy (FDA-approved 2023; slow the lesion but don’t improve vision; FDA-approved but NOT recommended by NICE — not available on the NHS for geographic atrophy)
🔴 Wet AMD
  • Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections — the mainstay + sight-saving
  • Ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab (off-label) (+ newer faricimab, brolucizumab) — block VEGF → halt neovascularisation + leakage
  • Loading course then maintenance (“treat-and-extend” / PRN, guided by OCT)
  • Early treatment preserves vision → urgency of referral
  • Photodynamic therapy (verteporfin) + laser — older, largely superseded
  • Urgent referral to a rapid-access macular clinic
Exam Pearls
What it is
Degeneration of the macula → loss of CENTRAL vision (peripheral spared); leading cause of irreversible blindness in the elderly.
Dry (~85–90%)
Drusen, geographic atrophy, gradual loss, no cure (AREDS2 vitamins slow progression; smoking cessation).
Wet (~10–15%)
Choroidal neovascularisation, VEGF-driven, sudden distortion/loss — TREATABLE with anti-VEGF.
Symptoms
Metamorphopsia (wavy lines) + central scotoma; test with Amsler grid.
Investigation
Key = OCT (fluid, drusen, membranes). FFA confirms neovascular membrane in wet AMD.
Hallmark
Drusen = yellow macular deposits.
Wet treatment
Urgent referral → intravitreal anti-VEGF (ranibizumab/aflibercept/bevacizumab/faricimab).
Risk / new Rx
Smoking = biggest modifiable risk. New complement inhibitors (pegcetacoplan/avacincaptad) slow geographic atrophy in dry AMD.
vs glaucoma
Peripheral vision preserved — patients not totally blind (vs glaucoma = peripheral loss).
OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conjunctivitis:
What & Why

Allergic conjunctivitis is a type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity inflammation of the conjunctiva in response to an allergen. It’s extremely common (often alongside allergic rhinitis — “hay fever eyes”), the key itchy, bilateral, watery red eye that must be distinguished from the dangerous causes of a red eye, and a simple stepwise treatment controls most cases.

The core mechanism: allergen contacts the conjunctiva → binds IgE on mast cells → degranulation → histamine release → itch, redness, watering, swelling. This is why antihistamines (block the effect) + mast-cell stabilisers (prevent the release) are the treatments.

Pain, photophobia, reduced vision, or an abnormal pupil are NOT features of allergic conjunctivitis — their presence means you must exclude keratitis, anterior uveitis, scleritis, or acute angle-closure glaucoma.

  • Seasonal (SAC) — commonest; pollen (grass, tree) → spring/summer (“hay fever”); often with allergic rhinitis
  • Perennial — year-round; house dust mite, animal dander, mould
  • Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) — more severe, chronic, in children/young males, with large “cobblestone” giant papillae under the upper lid; can threaten sight (corneal involvement) → specialist care
  • Atopic keratoconjunctivitis — adults with atopic dermatitis; chronic, sight-threatening
  • Giant papillary conjunctivitis — associated with contact lenses/sutures/prostheses
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Lid-eversion photo of “cobblestone” giant papillae under the upper tarsal conjunctiva, with chemosis (boggy conjunctival oedema)
  • Bilateral itching — the dominant, most specific symptom
  • Watery / stringy mucoid discharge; red, injected conjunctiva
  • Chemosis (conjunctival oedema — a swollen, “boggy”, sometimes gelatinous conjunctiva)
  • Eyelid swelling, tearing; often associated rhinitis + personal/family atopy (asthma, eczema, hay fever)
  • On lid eversion: papillae (cobblestone appearance, especially VKC)
Investigations
  • Clinical diagnosis — history (itch, bilateral, atopy, seasonality) + examination usually sufficient
  • No routine tests needed
  • Consider allergy testing (skin-prick/RAST) if the trigger is unclear or symptoms severe/persistent
  • Refer if diagnosis uncertain, red flags present, or severe/sight-threatening forms (VKC/atopic) suspected
Management (NICE CKS)
📷 Image placeholder — Stepwise ladder — allergen avoidance + cool compresses/lubricants → topical antihistamine/dual-action (relief) or mast-cell stabiliser (prophylaxis, start before season) → oral antihistamine → specialist-only steroids
Stepwise — allergen avoidance first, then topical drugs, escalating with severity.
1️⃣ General / non-pharmacological
  • Allergen avoidance (the foundation — reduce pollen/dust-mite/animal exposure)
  • Cool compresses, artificial tears/lubricants (dilute + wash out allergen, soothe)
  • Avoid eye rubbing; avoid contact lenses during flares
2️⃣ Topical treatments
  • Topical antihistamines (azelastine, olopatadine, ketotifen — many dual-action antihistamine + mast-cell stabiliser) — first-line, rapid relief, good for acute/intermittent
  • Topical mast-cell stabilisers (sodium cromoglicate, nedocromil, lodoxamide) — prophylactic: prevent degranulation but don’t relieve established symptoms + take days–weeks → start before the season
  • Oral antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine) — if associated rhinitis / systemic allergy
3. Severe/resistant: a short course of topical corticosteroid — only under specialist/ophthalmology supervision (risk of raised IOP/glaucoma, cataract, and worsening herpetic keratitis — never prescribe steroid drops for a red eye without excluding these). Vernal/atopic keratoconjunctivitis → specialist management (topical steroids, ciclosporin).
Exam Pearls
What it is
Type I IgE/mast-cell hypersensitivity → ITCHY, BILATERAL, WATERY red eye.
Hallmark
Itch; bilateral; associated with atopy/rhinitis (hay fever).
Red flags
NO pain, photophobia, reduced vision, or abnormal pupil — if present, exclude keratitis/uveitis/scleritis/AACG.
Sign
Chemosis (conjunctival oedema) + eyelid swelling are characteristic.
Types
Seasonal (pollen), perennial (dust mite/dander), vernal (children, cobblestone papillae, sight-threatening), giant papillary (contact lenses).
Diagnosis
Clinical — no routine tests.
Management
Allergen avoidance + cool compresses/lubricants → topical antihistamine/dual-action (relief) or mast-cell stabilisers (prophylaxis, slow onset) → oral antihistamine if rhinitis.
Steroids
Topical steroids only under specialist care (glaucoma/cataract/herpes risk).
Key distinction
Mast-cell stabilisers PREVENT but don’t RELIEVE — start early.
OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Conjunctivitis:
What & Why

Bacterial conjunctivitis is a bacterial infection of the conjunctiva — one of the three common causes of the “red eye” (with viral + allergic). It’s very common and, while mostly benign and self-limiting, a few presentations are sight- or life-threatening: gonococcal, chlamydial, neonatal, and contact-lens-related.

The core skill: most acute infective conjunctivitis is a self-limiting nuisance — the job is spotting the minority that isn’t (and reassuring the rest).

All three share: red eye, normal vision, no significant pain, no photophobia, normal pupil. If any of those red flags are present → think keratitis, uveitis, scleritis, or acute angle-closure glaucoma, not simple conjunctivitis.
Causative Organisms
📷 Image placeholder — Hyperacute copious purulent gonococcal conjunctivitis — the “over hours” sight-threatening presentation demanding systemic ceftriaxone and urgent referral
  • Common (adults/children): Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (esp. children), Moraxella
  • Contact-lens wearers: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Gram-negative) — high risk of keratitis/corneal ulcer; also Acanthamoeba
  • Gonococcal (N. gonorrhoeae) — hyperacute, copious purulent discharge, rapidly sight-threatening (corneal perforation)
  • Chlamydial (C. trachomatis) — chronic/subacute; trachoma (serotypes A–C) is the world’s leading infective cause of blindness
Clinical Features
  • Red, gritty, “sore” eye (foreign-body sensation, not true pain)
  • Purulent/mucopurulent discharge — eyelids crusted/stuck together in the morning (the classic); re-accumulates within minutes of wiping (vs watery viral)
  • Usually starts in one eye, spreads to the other
  • Vision normal (may transiently blur, clears on blinking); no significant pain/photophobia; pupil normal
  • Conjunctival injection (diffuse, more toward the fornices)
Investigations
  • Clinical diagnosis — history + examination; no tests for routine cases
  • Swabs for MC&S (+ chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT) — for severe/hyperacute, suspected gonococcal/chlamydial, neonatal, contact-lens wearers, immunocompromised, or treatment failure
  • Fluorescein staining if corneal involvement suspected (rule out ulcer/keratitis — especially contact-lens wearers)
Management (NICE CKS)
📷 Image placeholder — Flowchart — mild self-limiting case (hygiene + delayed chloramphenicol) branching to the four refer-now situations: contact-lens/keratitis, gonococcal, chlamydial, neonatal
Most cases are self-limiting — supportive care is first-line; antibiotics often unnecessary.
1️⃣ General / self-care (all)
  • Reassurance: most resolves within 5–7 days without treatment
  • Bathe/clean lids with cotton wool + cooled boiled water/saline to remove crusts
  • Hygiene — hand-washing, don’t share towels/pillows (contagious); avoid eye-rubbing + contact lenses until resolved
  • School/work exclusion not routinely required (UKHSA)
2️⃣ Topical antibiotics (if severe/not settling)
  • Chloramphenicol (0.5% drops / 1% ointment) — first-line, broad-spectrum, OTC. A delayed prescription (start if not improving after ~3 days) is reasonable
  • Fusidic acid — alternative (no Gram-negative cover); useful in pregnancy
  • Chloramphenicol cautions: avoid in prior myelosuppression/blood dyscrasia; avoid in pregnancy (use fusidic acid)
Special situations — refer/treat systemically: Contact-lens wearers with a red eye → stop lenses + low threshold to refer (exclude microbial keratitis / Pseudomonas / Acanthamoeba). Gonococcal → systemic ceftriaxone + urgent ophthalmology. Chlamydial → systemic azithromycin/doxycycline + GUM referral/contact tracing (it’s an STI). Neonatal (ophthalmia neonatorum, first 28 days) → ALWAYS refer urgently — gonococcal (within 48 h, sight-threatening) or chlamydial (5–14 days), from the maternal genital tract.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Purulent, sticky red eye; lids stuck together in the morning; usually starts unilateral.
Red flags
Vision normal, no significant pain/photophobia, pupil normal — if these are abnormal → exclude keratitis/uveitis/scleritis/AACG.
Organisms
Staph, Strep, Haemophilus (children); Pseudomonas in contact-lens wearers (keratitis risk); gonococcus (hyperacute), chlamydia (chronic/trachoma).
Course
Mostly self-limiting → resolves in 5–7 days; supportive care + hygiene first-line.
Antibiotics
Topical chloramphenicol if severe/not settling (delayed prescription reasonable); fusidic acid if pregnant.
Contact lens
Contact lens + red eye → stop lenses + refer (Pseudomonas/Acanthamoeba keratitis).
STI causes
Gonococcal → systemic ceftriaxone; chlamydial → azithromycin/doxycycline + GUM.
Neonatal
Ophthalmia neonatorum → ALWAYS refer (gonococcal <48 h; chlamydial 5–14 days).
Distinguish
vs viral (watery, preauricular node, URTI) and allergic (itchy, bilateral, atopy).
OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts:
What & Why

A cataract is an opacification (clouding) of the normally transparent crystalline lens. It’s the leading cause of blindness worldwide and the commonest treatable cause of visual impairment — and cataract surgery is the most frequently performed operation in the NHS and one of the most successful in medicine.

The core mechanism: the lens is kept clear by orderly proteins (crystallins). With ageing + oxidative stress (or metabolic/toxic insults) these proteins denature and aggregate, scattering light → the lens clouds → light can’t focus cleanly on the retina → blurred vision, glare, dimmed colours.
The Decisive Fork — Age-Related vs Secondary/Congenital
Age-related (senile)Secondary / congenital
CommonestYes — ageing + oxidative stress—
Secondary causes—Diabetes, corticosteroids, trauma, uveitis, radiation, high myopia, previous eye surgery
Congenital—Present at birth — detect early (absent red reflex); causes: intrauterine infection (rubella), galactosaemia, Down syndrome, hereditary
Types (by location in the lens)
📷 Image placeholder — Cataract types by lens location — nuclear (myopic “second sight”), cortical (glare) and posterior subcapsular (steroids/diabetes, disproportionate glare + near difficulty, progresses fastest)
  • Nuclear sclerotic — central lens; commonest age-related; causes a myopic shift (“second sight” — some elderly transiently read without glasses)
  • Cortical — spoke-like wedge opacities from the periphery; prominent glare
  • Posterior subcapsular — back of the lens; associated with steroids + diabetes; disproportionate glare + near-vision difficulty, progresses faster
Risk Factors
  • Increasing age (the dominant factor)
  • Smoking + high alcohol intake
  • Diabetes mellitus (+ metabolic disorders)
  • Corticosteroids (systemic or topical — the classic drug cause)
  • UV/sunlight, ionising radiation; ocular trauma, previous intraocular surgery, uveitis; high myopia; congenital/hereditary + intrauterine infection
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — An absent red reflex in a neonate = congenital cataract until proven otherwise → URGENT referral (part of the NIPE/6-week check)
  • Gradual, painless loss/blurring of vision (months–years)
  • Glare — bright lights, night headlights, haloes; faded/yellowed colours; reduced contrast sensitivity
  • Monocular diplopia (occasionally); myopic shift (nuclear); usually bilateral but asymmetric
On examination: Loss of the red reflex (or a dark opacity silhouetted against it) — the key sign. An absent red reflex in a neonate = congenital cataract → URGENT referral (part of the newborn/6-week check). Reduced acuity; the lens may look cloudy/grey (advanced).
Investigations
  • Clinical diagnosis — visual acuity + slit-lamp examination (grades + localises) + red reflex/ophthalmoscopy
  • Pre-operative: biometry (measures the eye to calculate the intraocular lens power); assess co-existing eye disease (glaucoma, AMD, diabetic retinopathy — which limit visual benefit)
  • Congenital cataract → investigate the cause (TORCH screen, galactosaemia, metabolic/genetic work-up)
Management (NICE)
📷 Image placeholder — NICE — do NOT ration surgery on visual acuity alone; offer phacoemulsification + IOL when the cataract affects quality of life after discussing risks/benefits
No medical treatment reverses or halts cataract — surgery is the only cure. Interim: stronger glasses / brighter reading lights may help mild cataract; modify risk factors (stop smoking, glycaemic control).
🔬 Surgery — definitive
  • Phacoemulsification — ultrasound emulsifies + aspirates the cloudy lens through a small incision; an artificial intraocular lens (IOL) is implanted
  • Usually day-case under local anaesthetic
  • Intracameral cefuroxime given to prevent endophthalmitis
📋 Referral criteria (NICE)
  • Do NOT restrict access on visual acuity alone
  • Offer surgery when the cataract affects quality of life (after discussing risks/benefits) — a functional decision, not a fixed acuity cut-off
  • Second-eye surgery uses the same criteria; bilateral simultaneous surgery considered in selected low-risk patients
Complications of surgery: Endophthalmitis — rare but serious intraocular infection (painful red eye + visual loss days after surgery) → sight-threatening emergency, urgent referral. Posterior capsule opacification (PCO) — the commonest late complication (“secondary cataract”): the capsule behind the IOL clouds months–years later → treated with YAG laser capsulotomy (quick, effective). Also: posterior capsule rupture (intraoperative), retinal detachment, cystoid macular oedema, IOL dislocation, raised IOP.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Clouding of the lens; leading cause of blindness worldwide; commonest cause = ageing/oxidative stress.
Presentation
Gradual PAINLESS blurring + glare/haloes + faded colours; usually bilateral, asymmetric.
Key sign
Loss of the red reflex — absent red reflex in a neonate = congenital cataract → URGENT referral.
Types
Nuclear (myopic shift, “second sight”), cortical (glare), posterior subcapsular (steroids/diabetes, fast, glare).
Risk factors
Age, smoking, diabetes, CORTICOSTEROIDS, UV, trauma, high myopia.
Treatment
No medical cure → surgery (phacoemulsification + IOL).
NICE
Don’t refuse surgery on visual acuity alone — decide on quality-of-life impact.
Complications
Endophthalmitis (emergency), posterior capsule opacification (commonest late → YAG laser).
Congenital causes
Rubella, galactosaemia, Down syndrome.
OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retinal Artery Oc:
What & Why

CRAO is sudden occlusion of the central retinal artery → acute ischaemia of the inner retina → sudden, painless, profound loss of vision in one eye. It’s a “stroke of the eye” — the ocular equivalent of an ischaemic cerebral stroke — and a warning of imminent stroke and cardiovascular events. Vision is often lost permanently, so the modern emphasis has shifted to treating the patient as a stroke (urgent work-up + secondary prevention) and not missing giant cell arteritis (treatable → saves the other eye).

The core anatomy: the central retinal artery (a branch of the ophthalmic artery → first branch of the internal carotid) supplies the inner retina. Occlusion → inner retinal infarction → pale/oedematous retina. The fovea is thin and shows the underlying choroidal circulation through it → the classic “cherry-red spot”.

Always ask about GCA symptoms + check ESR/CRP in any patient >50 with CRAO — missing arteritic CRAO risks rapid, bilateral, irreversible blindness.

  • Cardiac emboli — AF, valvular disease, endocarditis, post-MI mural thrombus
  • Hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, smoking
  • Hypercoagulable states, vasculitis, sickle cell
🔥 Arteritic
  • Giant cell (temporal) arteritis — the key one to exclude
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Fundus of CRAO — a diffusely pale, oedematous retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea and thread-like, attenuated arteries (“cattle-trucking”)
  • Sudden, painless, severe loss of vision in ONE eye — often “counting fingers” or worse; may be complete
  • May be preceded by amaurosis fugax (transient “curtain” visual loss → suggests a carotid embolic source)
  • Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) — the affected pupil dilates on the swinging-light test
Fundoscopy: pale, oedematous (“whitened”) retina with a “cherry-red spot” at the fovea (the classic sign); attenuated (thread-like) arteries, segmentation of the blood column (“cattle-trucking”); a visible embolus may be seen at a bifurcation (Hollenhorst plaque).
Investigations (treat it like a stroke)
  • Urgent ESR + CRP (± temporal artery biopsy) — exclude giant cell arteritis (immediately in >50s)
  • Bloods: FBC, glucose/HbA1c, lipids, clotting
  • ECG (AF) + carotid Doppler ultrasound (carotid stenosis — embolic source + secondary-prevention target); echocardiogram if cardiac source suspected
  • OCT (retinal oedema) + fundus fluorescein angiography (delayed arterial filling) confirm the diagnosis
  • Brain imaging as part of the stroke pathway; BP + vascular risk assessment
Management (emergency — treat as an acute stroke)
📷 Image placeholder — Emergency algorithm — exclude/treat GCA → low-evidence ocular measures (do not delay transfer) → consider IV thrombolysis <4.5h at a stroke centre → secondary prevention as the key long-term step
1️⃣ Exclude/treat GCA
  • If arteritic (GCA) suspected → immediate high-dose corticosteroids (IV methylprednisolone / high-dose oral prednisolone) before biopsy — to protect the fellow eye
2️⃣ Acute “eye” measures (low-evidence)
  • Ocular massage (intermittent digital globe pressure — may dislodge an embolus)
  • Lower IOP — IV acetazolamide ± mannitol, anterior chamber paracentesis
  • Inhaled carbogen/rebreathing (CO₂ → retinal vasodilation), sublingual GTN
  • Low-evidence — if a thrombolysis service is available, transfer takes priority over ocular massage
3. Thrombolysis (evolving): IV thrombolysis (tPA/alteplase) within a narrow early window (~<4.5 hours) is increasingly considered at stroke centres — recent meta-analyses suggest benefit with early treatment — but it remains not universally established. Manage within a stroke-pathway framework.
4. Secondary prevention (the most important long-term step): treat as a TIA/stroke — antiplatelet therapy, manage carotid stenosis (endarterectomy if significant), anticoagulate AF, control BP/lipids/diabetes, smoking cessation. This prevents the next (cerebral) stroke or MI — the real threat to the patient.
Complications
  • Permanent visual loss (the usual outcome — ~80% counting-fingers or worse)
  • Ocular neovascularisation → neovascular glaucoma, vitreous haemorrhage (retinal ischaemia drives VEGF) → follow up ~monthly for up to ~4 months
  • Subsequent stroke/MI — the systemic danger
Exam Pearls
What it is
“Stroke of the eye”: sudden, painless, profound MONOCULAR visual loss + RAPD.
Fundoscopy
Pale oedematous retina + CHERRY-RED SPOT at the fovea; thread-like arteries; ± visible embolus.
Must-not-miss
Always exclude GIANT CELL ARTERITIS in >50s (ESR/CRP; ask about headache/jaw claudication) → immediate high-dose steroids if suspected (saves the other eye).
Commonest cause
Carotid embolus (± cardiac, e.g. AF). May follow amaurosis fugax.
Manage as stroke
Urgent referral, stroke-pathway work-up (carotid Doppler, ECG/echo, brain imaging).
Acute Rx
Ocular massage / IV acetazolamide / lower IOP are low-evidence; thrombolysis (<4.5 h) increasingly considered at stroke centres.
Long-term
Secondary prevention (antiplatelet, carotid, AF, risk factors) is the key goal — prevents the next stroke/MI.
Cherry-red spot DDx
CRAO (elderly, acute) vs Tay-Sachs/storage diseases (infants).
vs CRVO
The venous counterpart = “blood and thunder” fundus, not a pale retina.
OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retinal Vein Occl:
What & Why

CRVO is thrombotic occlusion of the central retinal vein → blockage of venous drainage → back-pressure causing widespread retinal haemorrhage, oedema, and (if severe) ischaemia. It’s a common cause of sudden painless visual loss in older adults; its complications — macular oedema (main cause of visual loss, treatable with anti-VEGF) and neovascular glaucoma (ischaemic type) — are both preventable/treatable with prompt management. It’s the venous counterpart to CRAO.

The core mechanism (contrast with CRAO): CRAO is arterial (no blood in → pale retina). CRVO is venous (blood can’t get out → back-pressure → the retina engorges, haemorrhages + swells). The thrombus forms where the central retinal vein shares a sheath with the stiff atherosclerotic central retinal artery at the lamina cribrosa → this is why CRVO shares arterial risk factors (hypertension, atherosclerosis) despite being a venous event.
The Decisive Fork — Ischaemic vs Non-Ischaemic

Non-ischaemic (~75%)Ischaemic (~25%)
SeverityMilderSevere

Why it matters: the ischaemic type drives VEGF release → neovascularisation of the iris/angle → neovascular glaucoma (“90-day glaucoma”) + vitreous haemorrhage. Non-ischaemic CRVO can convert to ischaemic → all need monitoring.
Risk Factors
  • Increasing age (>50 — the majority)
  • Hypertension (the commonest — + atherosclerosis)
  • Hyperlipidaemia, diabetes, smoking
  • Raised intraocular pressure / glaucoma (a specific CRVO risk factor)
  • Hyperviscosity / thrombophilia — polycythaemia, myeloma, antiphospholipid syndrome (consider in younger patients)
  • Inflammatory / vasculitic (Behçet’s, sarcoidosis), oral contraceptive pill (younger patients)
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Colour fundus of a classic “blood and thunder” CRVO — flame/blot haemorrhages in all four quadrants, dilated tortuous veins, cotton-wool spots and macular/disc oedema
  • Sudden, painless loss/blurring of vision in ONE eye — variable severity (mild blurring → profound loss); often noticed on waking (venous stasis overnight)
  • RAPD if ischaemic (marker of severity)
Fundoscopy — the classic picture: “blood and thunder” fundus — widespread flame + blot haemorrhages in all four quadrants (the hallmark); dilated, tortuous veins; cotton-wool spots; optic disc swelling + macular oedema.
Contrast: branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) → haemorrhages confined to one sector/quadrant drained by the blocked branch, classically at an arteriovenous crossing.
Investigations
  • Fundoscopy / slit-lamp — the diagnosis is largely clinical
  • OCT — quantifies macular oedema (key for guiding + monitoring treatment)
  • Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) — assesses capillary non-perfusion → classifies ischaemic vs non-ischaemic (best once haemorrhage clears)
  • Systemic work-up: BP, fasting glucose/HbA1c, lipids, FBC (polycythaemia/hyperviscosity), ESR; intraocular pressure. In young / bilateral / recurrent → thrombophilia + inflammatory screen (antiphospholipid, protein C/S, myeloma, autoimmune)
Management (RCOphth)
1️⃣ Macular oedema (main treatable cause of visual loss)
  • Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections (ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab, faricimab) — first-line / gold-standard; improve vision + reduce oedema. Early treatment = better outcomes
  • Intravitreal steroids (dexamethasone implant / triamcinolone) — second-line/adjunct (risk of cataract + raised IOP)
  • Macular grid laser is NOT recommended for CRVO macular oedema — reduces leakage on angiography but no visual benefit (CVOS; unlike BRVO)
2️⃣ Neovascularisation / ischaemic CRVO
  • Pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP) — laser to ablate ischaemic retina, reducing VEGF drive → for neovascularisation of the iris/angle/retina (prevents/treats neovascular glaucoma); anti-VEGF is a useful adjunct
  • Monitor closely for neovascularisation (esp. ischaemic) — review ~1–2 monthly in the first year
3. Systemic: treat cardiovascular risk factors — control BP, lipids, diabetes; smoking cessation — reduces risk to the fellow eye (shared vascular risk). Address any hyperviscosity/thrombophilia/inflammatory cause in younger patients. Like CRAO, CRVO is a marker of systemic vascular disease.
Complications
📷 Image placeholder — Rubeosis iridis / neovascular (“90-day”) glaucoma — iris and angle new vessels following ischaemic CRVO
  • Macular oedema — the commonest cause of visual loss
  • Neovascular glaucoma — from iris/angle neovascularisation (ischaemic type) — painful, sight-threatening (“90-day glaucoma”)
  • Vitreous haemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment (from neovascularisation)
  • Macular ischaemia — permanent central visual loss
Exam Pearls
Fundoscopy
CRVO = “blood and thunder” fundus (widespread haemorrhages all 4 quadrants) + dilated tortuous veins + cotton-wool spots + macular oedema.
Presentation
Sudden, PAINLESS, monocular visual loss — variable severity; often on waking.
The fork
Ischaemic (~25%, poor vision, RAPD, >10 DA non-perfusion) vs non-ischaemic (~75%, better vision). Non-ischaemic can CONVERT to ischaemic.
Dreaded complication
Ischaemic CRVO → VEGF → neovascularisation → NEOVASCULAR GLAUCOMA (“90-day glaucoma”) + vitreous haemorrhage.
Risk factors
Age, HYPERTENSION, atherosclerosis, diabetes, glaucoma, hyperviscosity (young → thrombophilia screen).
Investigations
OCT (macular oedema), FFA (ischaemic vs non-ischaemic); systemic vascular work-up.
Macular oedema Rx
Anti-VEGF (1st-line); steroids 2nd-line; macular grid laser NOT beneficial in CRVO.
Neovascularisation
Pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP). Treat vascular risk factors (marker of systemic vascular disease).
Contrast
CRAO = pale retina + cherry-red spot (arterial); CRVO = blood-and-thunder (venous); BRVO = one sector only.
OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-Angle Glauco:
What & Why

Chronic open-angle glaucoma is a progressive optic neuropathy — characteristic optic-nerve-head damage with corresponding visual field loss — usually (not always) associated with raised intraocular pressure (IOP). It’s the commonest glaucoma and a leading cause of irreversible blindness — and critically it is asymptomatic until advanced (painless, gradual, peripheral field loss the patient doesn’t notice until central vision is threatened). It’s a disease found by screening; early detection + IOP-lowering prevents blindness, but damage already done is permanent. The chronic, painless counterpart to acute angle-closure.

The core mechanism: aqueous drains through the trabecular meshwork at the (open, normal-looking) angle. In POAG there is increased resistance to outflow through an anatomically OPEN angle → IOP rises (or the nerve is susceptible even at “normal” pressure) → pressure damages retinal ganglion cell axons at the optic nerve head → disc cupping + arcuate/peripheral field defects.

Chronic Open-Angle (POAG)Acute Angle-Closure (AACG)

Risk Factors
  • Increasing age (the dominant factor)
  • Raised IOP (the major modifiable risk factor)
  • Family history (first-degree relative — strong; screen relatives)
  • Ethnicity — Black/African-Caribbean (earlier, more aggressive) (contrast: angle-closure commoner in East Asians)
  • Myopia; diabetes, hypertension; corticosteroid use (steroid-responders)
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Fundus photo of glaucomatous disc cupping — an increased cup:disc ratio (>0.5) with neuroretinal-rim thinning and a disc haemorrhage
  • Asymptomatic in early disease — the key point; patients don’t notice gradual peripheral loss
  • Gradual, painless loss of PERIPHERAL vision → “tunnel vision” in advanced disease (central vision preserved until late — opposite of AMD)
  • May present with missing patches, difficulty in low light, or bumping into things; often detected on a routine optician visit
Examination — the diagnostic triad: (1) raised IOP (though “normal-tension glaucoma” exists — damage at normal IOP); (2) optic disc cupping — increased cup-to-disc ratio (>0.5, or asymmetry), neuroretinal rim thinning, vessel “bayoneting”, notching, disc haemorrhages; (3) visual field defects — arcuate scotomas, nasal step → peripheral constriction.
Investigations (NICE)
📷 Image placeholder — Humphrey visual-field printout — an arcuate scotoma / nasal step progressing to peripheral constriction (tunnel vision) with the central field preserved until late
  • Goldmann applanation tonometry — measure IOP (the standard)
  • Gonioscopy — confirms the angle is OPEN (distinguishes from angle-closure)
  • Visual field testing (perimetry) — maps + monitors field loss
  • Optic nerve assessment — fundoscopy/OCT of the disc + retinal nerve fibre layer (cupping, rim thinning)
  • Central corneal thickness (pachymetry) — a thin cornea underestimates true IOP (+ is an independent risk factor)
Management (NICE)
📷 Image placeholder — Treatment ladder — 360° selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) first-line (LiGHT trial, NICE 2022) → latanoprost drops → beta-blocker/carbonic-anhydrase-inhibitor/alpha-agonist → trabeculectomy
Aim: lower IOP to slow/halt progression + preserve remaining vision (damage already done is irreversible).
First-line — 360° Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (SLT): a major 2022 change — NICE now recommends offering 360° SLT as initial treatment for newly diagnosed COAG (and ocular hypertension with IOP ≥24 mmHg), based on the LiGHT trial. Laser to the trabecular meshwork improves outflow + can delay or avoid eye drops.
💧 Medical (drops — if SLT declined/unsuitable, or add-on)
  • Prostaglandin analogue (latanoprost) — first-line drug; ↑uveoscleral outflow; once-daily. Side effects: iris/periocular pigmentation, eyelash growth, conjunctival hyperaemia
  • Beta-blocker (timolol) — ↓production (caution asthma/COPD/bradycardia)
  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (dorzolamide; oral acetazolamide) — ↓production
  • Alpha-2 agonist (brimonidine) — ↓production + ↑outflow; miotics (pilocarpine) — ↑outflow (less used)
🔪 Surgical

  • MIGS (minimally invasive glaucoma surgery), drainage tubes/shunts — increasingly used

What it is
Chronic, PAINLESS, progressive optic neuropathy with an OPEN angle → gradual PERIPHERAL field loss (“tunnel vision”), asymptomatic until late.
Diagnostic triad
Raised IOP + optic disc CUPPING (↑cup:disc ratio) + visual field defect (arcuate scotoma/nasal step).
Normal-tension
“Normal-tension glaucoma” = typical damage at normal IOP (exists).
Risk factors
Age, raised IOP, family history, Black ethnicity, myopia, diabetes.
Investigations
Tonometry (IOP), gonioscopy (open angle), perimetry (fields), OCT/fundoscopy (disc), pachymetry.
1st-line (NICE 2022)
360° selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT). Then/or prostaglandin analogue (latanoprost) → beta-blocker/CAI/alpha-agonist → trabeculectomy.
Latanoprost SEs
Iris pigmentation, eyelash growth.
Key point
Vision loss is IRREVERSIBLE — treatment prevents further loss. Lifelong monitoring; screen relatives; DVLA if fields affected.

vs AACG: open vs closed angle, chronic/painless vs acute/painful, peripheral vs sudden loss.
OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Retinopathy:
What & Why

Diabetic retinopathy is a microvascular complication of diabetes in which chronic hyperglycaemia damages the retinal blood vessels → leakage, ischaemia, and (ultimately) abnormal new-vessel growth. It’s a leading cause of blindness in the working-age population (16–64) in the UK, largely preventable with good control + detectable early by screening, and its sight-threatening stages (proliferative + maculopathy) are treatable if caught in time. Every diabetic is screened precisely because it’s asymptomatic until it threatens sight.

The core mechanism: persistent hyperglycaemia damages the retinal capillary endothelium + pericytes → vessels become leaky (haemorrhages, exudates, oedema) and occluded (retinal ischaemia). Ischaemic retina releases VEGF → neovascularisation (fragile new vessels that bleed + scar). This leak-then-ischaemia-then-neovascularisation sequence explains the whole staging.
The Decisive Fork — Retinopathy (R) vs Maculopathy (M)

Two axes are graded separately — retinopathy (R) and maculopathy (M) — because maculopathy threatens central vision independently of the retinopathy stage.

R1Background (non-proliferative)Microaneurysms, dot/blot haemorrhages, hard exudates
R2Pre-proliferativeCotton-wool spots (ischaemia), venous beading, IRMA, deeper haemorrhages

Types of maculopathy: focal/diffuse exudative (leakage); ischaemic (macular capillary non-perfusion — poorer prognosis); clinically significant macular oedema (CSMO) — the treatment threshold.

  • Duration of diabetes (the biggest — most type 1 have some retinopathy after ~20 years)
  • Poor glycaemic control (high HbA1c); hypertension; hyperlipidaemia
  • Pregnancy (can accelerate — needs extra screening); renal disease, smoking
  • Rapid tightening of glucose control can cause transient early worsening — warn patients
Clinical Features
  • Asymptomatic in early stages — hence screening
  • Gradual reduction in visual acuity (especially maculopathy — central/reading vision)
  • Floaters or sudden visual loss → suggests vitreous haemorrhage (from proliferative new vessels); distortion (maculopathy)
  • Fundoscopy signs map onto the grades (microaneurysms, dot/blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots, venous beading, IRMA, new vessels, pre-retinal/vitreous haemorrhage, fibrous proliferation)
Screening & Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — OCT of centre-involving diabetic macular oedema — increased central retinal thickness with intraretinal cystoid spaces (the treatment threshold)
  • UK Diabetic Eye Screening Programme: annual digital retinal photography through dilated pupils for all diabetics from age 12
  • OCT — the gold standard for detecting + monitoring macular oedema (quantifies retinal thickening)
  • Fundus fluorescein angiography — maps ischaemia + neovascularisation
  • Referral: R3 (proliferative) → urgent (~2 weeks); M1 / R2 → routine ophthalmology referral
Management (NICE)
📷 Image placeholder — Post pan-retinal photocoagulation fundus — the scattered peripheral laser-burn pattern that ablates ischaemic VEGF-producing retina and regresses new vessels
Two arms: control the systemic disease (prevention/slowing) + treat sight-threatening complications.
1️⃣ Systemic (all patients)
  • Optimise glycaemic control (HbA1c individualised, e.g. ~48–53 mmol/mol)
  • Blood pressure control (<140/80; a tighter <130/80 if kidney, eye or cerebrovascular damage — NICE)
  • Lipid management (statin), smoking cessation; extra screening in pregnancy
2️⃣ Proliferative (R3)
  • Pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP) — first-line; laser burns to the peripheral ischaemic retina ablate VEGF-producing tissue → new vessels regress
  • Side effects: peripheral field loss, reduced night vision/contrast (sacrifices peripheral retina to save central)
  • Anti-VEGF — second-line if active despite complete PRP; vitrectomy — for vitreous haemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment
3️⃣ Maculopathy / macular oedema
  • Intravitreal anti-VEGF (ranibizumab, aflibercept, faricimab) — first-line for centre-involving CSMO
  • Macular laser — default for non-centre-involving oedema
  • Intravitreal steroids (dexamethasone implant) — an option (cataract/IOP risk)
Complications
  • Vitreous haemorrhage (from proliferative new vessels) — sudden visual loss/floaters
  • Tractional retinal detachment (fibrous scaffolding contracts)
  • Neovascular glaucoma (iris/angle neovascularisation — “rubeosis iridis”)
  • Permanent visual loss / blindness

What it is
Microvascular complication of diabetes; a leading cause of blindness in working-age adults.
Mechanism
Hyperglycaemia → leaky + occluded retinal capillaries → ischaemia → VEGF → neovascularisation.
Grading

New vessels = proliferative = URGENT referral. Maculopathy = commonest cause of visual loss.

Annual digital retinal photography (dilated) from age 12. OCT = gold standard for macular oedema.
Systemic
Tight glucose + BP + lipids + smoking cessation. Rapid glucose lowering can transiently worsen retinopathy.

PRP first-line (anti-VEGF 2nd-line; vitrectomy for haemorrhage/detachment).

Anti-VEGF first-line (centre-involving); macular laser for non-centre-involving.
Complications
Vitreous haemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment, neovascular glaucoma (rubeosis).
OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simplex (HSV) Kera:
What & Why

Herpes simplex keratitis is corneal infection/inflammation caused by herpes simplex virus (usually HSV-1) — the commonest infective cause of corneal blindness in the developed world. It’s a sight-threatening cause of the painful red eye, it recurs, and — the single most important teaching point — topical corticosteroids given for the epithelial (dendritic) form dramatically worsen it and can cause corneal perforation. It’s the classic reason never to give steroid drops for an undiagnosed red eye.

The core mechanism: after primary infection, HSV-1 lies latent in the trigeminal ganglion. Triggers (UV/sunlight, illness/fever, stress, immunosuppression, menstruation, steroids) cause reactivation → the virus travels down the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1) to the cornea → replicates in the epithelium → the characteristic branching dendritic ulcer. Repeated episodes drive stromal scarring + vision loss.
The Decisive Fork — Epithelial vs Stromal Disease

Only in stromal/disciform disease (immune-driven) are steroids used — and always with antiviral cover, under ophthalmology.

  • UV/sunlight exposure; fever/systemic illness; physical/emotional stress; menstruation
  • Immunosuppression (HIV, transplant, chemotherapy), atopic disease
  • Topical or systemic corticosteroids; contact lens wear, ocular surgery

📷 Image placeholder — Fluorescein-stained dendritic ulcer under cobalt-blue light — branching, serpentine, with terminal bulbs (pathognomonic of epithelial HSV keratitis)

  • Blurred vision (if central cornea/stroma involved)
  • Reduced corneal sensation (HSV damages corneal nerves — a useful clue)
  • May have vesicles on the eyelids/periocular skin

  • Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein — usually diagnostic (a dendrite confirms it); assess for stromal involvement
  • Corneal sensation testing (reduced in HSV)
  • Viral swab/PCR (corneal/conjunctival) — if uncertain or atypical
  • Any painful red eye → do NOT start steroid drops before slit-lamp + fluorescein exclude a dendritic ulcer

🦠 Epithelial (dendritic)

  • Epithelial debridement (specialist); cycloplegic (cyclopentolate) for comfort
  • Do NOT use topical corticosteroids (→ geographic ulcer/perforation)
🛡️ Stromal / disciform
  • Topical corticosteroid + antiviral cover — under ophthalmology supervision (immune-mediated, so steroids are needed here, but always with antiviral)

  • Geographic/amoeboid ulcer (especially steroid-induced) → corneal melt/perforation
  • Neurotrophic (metaherpetic) keratopathy — poor healing from corneal nerve damage; secondary bacterial infection, stromal neovascularisation

Commonest infective cause of corneal blindness; HSV-1 latent in the TRIGEMINAL ganglion, reactivates down V1.

Painful red eye + photophobia + watering + reduced corneal sensation.

Active virus → topical aciclovir/ganciclovir; steroids CONTRAINDICATED.
Stromal Rx
Immune-mediated → topical steroid + antiviral cover (ophthalmology).

NEVER give steroid drops for an undiagnosed red eye — fluorescein first to exclude a dendrite (steroids → geographic ulcer/perforation).
Triggers / prophylaxis
UV/sunlight, illness/fever, stress, immunosuppression, steroids, menstruation. Recurrent → prophylactic oral aciclovir.
Complications
Recurrence, corneal scarring/blindness, geographic ulcer/perforation, neurotrophic keratopathy.

OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive Retinopathy:
What & Why

Hypertensive retinopathy is retinal damage from chronic (or acutely severe) high blood pressure — the eye’s version of hypertensive target-organ damage. It matters because the retina is the only place you can directly see the effects of hypertension on blood vessels, the grade correlates with cardiovascular/stroke risk + mortality, and its most severe form (grade 4 / papilloedema) signals malignant (accelerated) hypertension — a medical emergency.

The core mechanism (three phases): (1) vasoconstrictive — arterioles constrict → generalised narrowing; (2) sclerotic — chronic pressure thickens the walls (arteriosclerosis) → copper/silver wiring + AV nipping (the thick artery compresses the vein where they cross); (3) exudative — the blood-retinal barrier breaks down → haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates, and (if severe) optic disc swelling. The grading follows this progression.
The Decisive Fork — Chronic vs Malignant (Emergency)

  • Arteriolar narrowing — generalised then focal
  • AV nipping (nicking) — the vein appears pinched/deviated where a thickened artery crosses it
  • Copper wiring → silver wiring — increasingly sclerotic arterioles reflect light abnormally (copper = moderate; silver = severe)
  • Cotton-wool spots — fluffy white patches = nerve-fibre-layer microinfarcts (ischaemia)
  • Flame haemorrhages — superficial nerve-fibre-layer bleeds
  • Hard exudates — lipid/protein leakage; a macular star when arranged around the fovea
  • Papilloedema — optic disc swelling (grade 4 / malignant)
Clinical Features & Investigations
  • Usually asymptomatic (found on routine fundoscopy)
  • Malignant hypertension: headache, visual disturbance/blurring, + features of other end-organ damage (AKI, heart failure, encephalopathy)
  • Sudden visual loss → suggests a complication (retinal vein/artery occlusion)
Investigations: blood pressure + fundoscopy / dilated fundus exam (grade the changes) drive the diagnosis. Assess other target-organ damage: urinalysis + U&Es (renal), ECG/echo (LVH); fundus photography/OCT/FFA for documentation. Screen for secondary hypertension if young/severe/resistant.
Management
The treatment is to control the blood pressure — not primarily an “eye” treatment.
🟢 Chronic (grades 1–3)
  • Manage hypertension per standard guidelines (lifestyle + antihypertensives — ACE inhibitor/ARB, calcium-channel blocker, thiazide-like diuretic, per NICE)
  • Address global cardiovascular risk (lipids, diabetes, smoking cessation)
  • Most retinal changes stabilise or improve with good BP control
🔴 Malignant (grade 4 — emergency)
  • Same-day specialist assessment/admission for severe hypertension (e.g. >180/120) with retinal haemorrhages/papilloedema or acute end-organ damage
  • Lower BP GRADUALLY — NOT too fast (reduce by no more than ~25% in the first 24 hours) → rapid reduction risks cerebral/retinal/renal ischaemia/infarction
  • Controllable agents (e.g. IV labetalol) with monitoring
Complications
  • Retinal vein or artery occlusion (hypertension is a major risk factor)
  • Macular oedema / exudative retinal detachment (severe cases)
  • Optic atrophy (prolonged papilloedema) → permanent visual loss
  • Worsening of co-existing diabetic retinopathy; marks elevated stroke/cardiac/renal risk
Exam Pearls
What it is
Retinal target-organ damage from high BP; the grade reflects systemic cardiovascular/stroke risk.
Three phases
Vasoconstrictive (narrowing) → sclerotic (AV nipping, copper/silver wiring) → exudative (haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates).
Keith-Wagener-Barker
G1 arteriolar narrowing → G2 + AV nipping/copper wiring → G3 + haemorrhages/cotton-wool spots/exudates (silver wiring) → G4 + PAPILLOEDEMA = malignant hypertension.
Signs
Cotton-wool spots = nerve-fibre-layer infarcts; macular star = hard exudates around the fovea.
Course
Usually asymptomatic — found on fundoscopy.
Emergency
Grade 4 / papilloedema = malignant hypertension → EMERGENCY, same-day; lower BP GRADUALLY (≤25% in 24 h) to avoid ischaemic infarction.
Management
Control BP + cardiovascular risk; changes often reverse with good control.
Complications
Retinal vein/artery occlusion, optic atrophy, worsens diabetic retinopathy.
Contrast
HTN = AV nipping, flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots; diabetes = microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages, neovascularisation.
OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detachment:
What & Why

Retinal detachment is separation of the neurosensory retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) — the light-sensing layer lifts off the tissue that nourishes it. It’s a time-critical, sight-threatening emergency: the detached retina loses its blood/nutrient supply and photoreceptors die within days → permanent vision loss if not repaired promptly.

The examinable essence: recognise the warning triad (flashes, floaters, a ‘curtain’), understand that “macula-on” vs “macula-off” determines urgency + visual prognosis, and know treatment is surgical.
The core anatomy: the neurosensory retina (photoreceptors) + the RPE (supplies it) are only loosely apposed, held together by vitreous pressure + RPE pumping. If fluid gets between them (through a tear, from traction, or by exudation), the retina detaches → photoreceptors lose RPE support → degenerate.
The Decisive Fork — Which Mechanism?
📷 Image placeholder — Three mechanisms — rhegmatogenous (a break lets vitreous fluid under the retina), tractional (a fibrous membrane pulls the retina off in diabetes) and exudative (fluid leak, no break/traction)
TypeMechanismTypical cause
Rhegmatogenous (commonest)A retinal break/tear lets vitreous fluid pass under the retinaPVD, myopia, trauma, previous cataract surgery, lattice degeneration
TractionalFibrous tissue pulls the retina offProliferative diabetic retinopathy, sickle cell, prior trauma
Exudative (serous)Fluid leaks under the retina (no break, no traction)Inflammation, tumour, malignant hypertension/pre-eclampsia, central serous retinopathy
“Rhegmatogenous” = from a rhegma (break) — the classic + commonest; the one that presents with flashes/floaters/curtain and needs urgent surgery.
Risk Factors (mainly rhegmatogenous)
  • Myopia (short-sightedness) — the biggest (longer, thinner eye/retina)
  • Posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) — the key precipitant (the ageing vitreous pulls on the retina → a tear)
  • Increasing age (50s–70s); previous cataract surgery (pseudophakia); ocular trauma
  • Previous retinal detachment (or in the other eye), family history; lattice degeneration; diabetic retinopathy (tractional)
Clinical Features — the Warning Triad
📷 Image placeholder — Patient’s-eye view — a dark curtain/shadow ascending across the peripheral field, with flashes (photopsia) and a shower of floaters (the painless warning triad)
  • Flashes (photopsia) — brief peripheral flashes of light (vitreous traction on the retina)
  • Floaters — a sudden increase/shower of black spots or a “cobweb”; a large single floater (Weiss ring) suggests PVD; a shower of tiny dots (“tobacco dust”/Shafer’s sign) suggests a tear
  • A “curtain”/“shadow” descending across the visual field — the area of detached retina (progressive, painless)
  • Painless loss of vision; central vision preserved until the macula detaches — once the macula goes, central acuity drops + a RAPD may appear in large detachments
Key distinction — PVD vs detachment: posterior vitreous detachment alone (very common, benign) also causes flashes + floaters — but a curtain/shadow or reduced vision suggests the PVD has caused a tear/detachment → refer. Any new flashes/floaters need assessment to exclude a break.
The Critical Concept — Macula-On vs Macula-Off
📷 Image placeholder — Subretinal fluid sparing the fovea (macula-on → operate within ~24h) vs fluid under the fovea (macula-off → central vision already lost)
🎯 Macula-ON (still attached, central vision intact)
  • EXTREMELY urgent — operate before the macula detaches to preserve central vision (best outcomes; ideally within ~24 h)
  • While waiting, posture the patient to keep fluid away from the macula
🌫️ Macula-OFF (already detached, central vision lost)
  • Still urgent, but the window is slightly less frantic (ideally within ~2–3 days)
  • Visual prognosis is already compromised — central vision often doesn’t fully recover
Investigations
  • Dilated fundus examination (indirect ophthalmoscopy) — the key test: shows the detached retina (grey, elevated, mobile), identifies breaks/tears, and whether the macula is on or off
  • Slit-lamp — pigment cells/“tobacco dust” in the anterior vitreous (Shafer’s sign)
  • B-scan ultrasound — if the view is obscured (vitreous haemorrhage/cataract)
  • OCT — assesses macular involvement (macula-on vs off); visual acuity + RAPD
Management (ophthalmic emergency)
Refer for same-day ophthalmology assessment for any suspected detachment. While awaiting surgery: posture the patient to keep subretinal fluid away from the macula (position depends on the break location); avoid strenuous activity.
🔧 Retinal tear / securing a break
  • Laser retinopexy or cryotherapy — seals the break to prevent (further) detachment
🔪 Established rhegmatogenous detachment
  • Pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) — removes vitreous, drains subretinal fluid, seals breaks, + gas or silicone oil tamponade (posture post-op); for complex/posterior breaks, pseudophakia, vitreous haemorrhage
  • Scleral buckling — a silicone band indents the sclera to reappose the retina + relieve traction; favoured in younger/phakic eyes / dialysis
  • Pneumatic retinopexy — an intraocular gas bubble tamponades a selected superior break (+ laser/cryo), under local anaesthetic
(Often combined; anatomical success ~85–90%.) Tractional/exudative types: treat the underlying cause — laser/vitrectomy for diabetic tractional detachment; BP control / treat tumour or inflammation for exudative.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Neurosensory retina separates from the RPE → photoreceptor death → permanent visual loss if not repaired promptly. EMERGENCY.
Triad
FLASHES (photopsia) + FLOATERS (sudden increase) + a CURTAIN/shadow across the field. PAINLESS.
Types
Rhegmatogenous (commonest — a break; PVD/myopia/trauma) / tractional (diabetic retinopathy) / exudative (inflammation, tumour, malignant HTN).
Risk factors
Myopia + posterior vitreous detachment are the key ones for rhegmatogenous RD.
Macula on/off
Macula-ON (central vision intact) = operate urgently to save central vision; macula-OFF = central vision already lost (worse prognosis).
Diagnosis
Dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy (grey elevated mobile retina, find the break); B-scan if view obscured; RAPD in large detachments.
Management
Same-day ophthalmology referral; posture to protect the macula while waiting. Laser/cryo for tears; vitrectomy / scleral buckle / pneumatic retinopexy for detachment.
Golden rule
New flashes/floaters → exclude a retinal tear (PVD alone is benign, but a curtain or reduced vision means refer).
OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / Episcleritis:
What & Why

Episcleritis and scleritis are inflammation of the outer coats of the eye — the episclera (thin vascular layer between conjunctiva and sclera) and the sclera (tough white outer wall). They present similarly (a red eye ± pain) but are worlds apart: episcleritis is a benign, self-limiting nuisance, whereas scleritis is a painful, sight-threatening emergency strongly linked to systemic autoimmune/vasculitic disease — and can be the first sign of life-threatening granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

The examinable skill: tell the two apart (the phenylephrine test) and know that scleritis mandates a systemic work-up.
The core distinction: episcleritis = superficial, mild, mobile vessels that blanch, minimal/no pain, self-limiting. Scleritis = deep, severe boring pain, immobile violaceous vessels that don’t blanch, systemic disease, refer urgently.

  • Mild/no pain (discomfort, watering, gritty)
  • No visual impairment, no discharge, minimal/no photophobia
  • Simple (diffuse/sectoral) or nodular (a mobile nodule) forms
  • Mostly idiopathic; sometimes mild autoimmune links — no systemic work-up for a single typical episode

  • Self-limiting — reassurance often all that’s needed (~1–2 weeks)
  • Lubricants (artificial tears) for comfort
  • Topical/oral NSAIDs if troublesome; topical steroids occasionally (specialist)

  • Globe tenderness; deep violaceous/bluish-red injection; may have reduced vision, photophobia, watering

  • Nodular (an immobile tender nodule — vs the mobile nodule of nodular episcleritis)

  • Necrotising WITHOUT inflammation (scleromalacia perforans) — painless scleral thinning in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis

  • Immunosuppression / biologics (methotrexate, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide or rituximab for necrotising/vasculitic disease) — under rheumatology
  • Treat the underlying systemic disease + any infective cause (e.g. antivirals for herpetic scleritis); topical steroids are adjunctive

Episcleritis
Superficial, MILD/painless, sectoral bright-red, self-limiting, idiopathic.
Scleritis
Deep, SEVERE boring pain (worse at night/on eye movement), violaceous hue, globe tender, ~50% systemic disease — EMERGENCY.

Reassurance ± lubricants/NSAIDs. No systemic work-up for a single episode.
Scleritis Rx
Urgent referral + systemic work-up (ESR/CRP, ANCA, RF, ANA, urinalysis) + systemic NSAIDs/steroids/immunosuppression.
Associations
Commonest = rheumatoid arthritis; scleritis can be the FIRST sign of GPA (Wegener’s)/vasculitis — don’t miss it.
Subtypes
Necrotising scleritis = most severe; scleromalacia perforans = painless thinning in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. Posterior scleritis → B-scan (T-sign).
Nodule
Episcleritis nodule is MOBILE; scleritis nodule is IMMOBILE.
OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iritis:
What & Why

Uveitis is inflammation of the uveal tract — the pigmented middle layer (iris, ciliary body, choroid). Anterior uveitis (iritis/iridocyclitis) — inflammation of the iris ± ciliary body — is the commonest form (~75%). It’s a leading cause of the painful red eye with photophobia, the classic HLA-B27 / seronegative spondyloarthropathy eye disease (a major rheumatology crossover), it recurs, and untreated it causes sight-threatening complications (posterior synechiae, glaucoma, cataract, macular oedema).

The core anatomy: the uvea = iris + ciliary body + choroid. Classified by site — anterior (iris/ciliary body — the focus), intermediate (vitreous), posterior (choroid/retina), or panuveitis. Anterior uveitis inflames the anterior chamber → white cells + protein leak in (breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier) → the hallmark signs.

Refer to ophthalmology (urgent/same-day for acute anterior uveitis). Aims: suppress inflammation, relieve pain, prevent synechiae/complications.

  • Monitor IOP and treat uveitic glaucoma

  • Band keratopathy (chronic — calcium in the cornea); vision loss

Topical STEROIDS + CYCLOPLEGIC (dilate to relieve pain + prevent/break synechiae). Systemic immunosuppression/anti-TNF (adalimumab) for severe/recurrent.
