Painful red eye + photophobia + hypopyon + inflammatory back pain = HLA-B27 uveitis + ankylosing spondylitis.
OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Examination:
Visual acuity (VA) is the vital sign of the eye — a single number that quantifies central foveal function and must be documented in every ocular presentation before anything else is done. The slit-lamp biomicroscope is the companion tool: a binocular microscope with a variable-width, variable-angle slit of light that gives a magnified, stereoscopic, optically-sectioned view of the anterior segment (lids, conjunctiva, cornea, anterior chamber, iris and lens) and, with an added condensing lens, the fundus. Together they answer the two first questions of any eye assessment: how well does this eye see and what does it look like under magnification.

1Indication & principle

VA is measured in every eye complaint (red eye, trauma, sudden or gradual visual loss, headache, medico-legal documentation). It screens the whole visual axis from tear film to cortex; a drop in acuity flags pathology needing explanation. The slit-lamp is used whenever the anterior segment must be examined in detail — foreign body, keratitis, anterior uveitis, cataract grading, IOP measurement (with applanation tonometry) and dilated fundal review.

📏Snellen VA
Distance test at 6 m; recorded as 6/6, 6/12 etc — numerator = test distance, denominator = distance a normal eye reads that line
🕳️Pinhole
Removes refractive error — if VA improves through a pinhole the deficit is refractive, not pathological
🔬Slit-lamp
Stereoscopic magnified beam optically sections the cornea & lens and illuminates the anterior chamber
📊LogMAR
Formal/research chart with equal letters per line & equal spacing — more accurate, lower score = better vision (0.0 = 6/6)
2How it is performed
VA: Patient sits 6 m from a well-lit Snellen chart (or 3 m with a mirror). Test each eye separately, occluding the other, with the patient wearing their usual distance glasses (record as “aided”). Ask them to read down to the smallest line they can.
Record the lowest line read as numerator/denominator, e.g. 6/6 (normal), 6/12. Note letters missed (e.g. 6/9-2). Then repeat with a pinhole to unmask refractive error.
If the top letter (6/60) cannot be read at 6 m, walk the patient forward and record the distance (e.g. 3/60), then step down to counting fingers (CF), hand movements (HM), and perception of light (PL / NPL).
Slit-lamp: Patient's chin on the rest, forehead against the band. Start with a moderate beam; use a narrow slit angled ~45° to optically section the cornea and lens, and a narrow tall beam in a dark room to look for cells/flare in the anterior chamber. Fluorescein highlights epithelial defects under cobalt-blue light. Add a +90 D condensing lens for a stereoscopic fundal view.
📷 Image placeholder — slit-lamp view of the anterior segment: a narrow angled beam optically sectioning a clear cornea, with a hazy “beam in a dark room” showing anterior-chamber cells and flare in acute anterior uveitis.
3Interpretation
VA improves markedly with pinhole→Uncorrected refractive error — refer to optometry, not urgent pathology
VA does NOT improve with pinhole→Organic pathology along the visual axis (media opacity, retinal or optic-nerve disease) — needs a cause
VA 6/6 or better→Normal central acuity
Sudden drop to CF / HM / PL→Sight-threatening event (e.g. central retinal artery occlusion, vitreous haemorrhage) — emergency
Cells & flare in the anterior chamber→Active anterior uveitis (inflammation) — protein & leucocytes leaking from an inflamed iris/ciliary body
Hazy cornea + fixed mid-dilated pupil + shallow AC→Acute angle-closure glaucoma — urgent
Fluorescein-staining epithelial defect→Corneal abrasion or ulcer (dendritic pattern → herpes simplex keratitis)
Lens opacity on retro-illumination→Cataract — grade and correlate with the acuity drop
4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Not recording pinhole VA is the commonest error — you cannot separate a simple refractive cause from disease without it.
Forgetting usual glasses falsely lowers acuity; always state aided vs unaided.
Snellen limitations: unequal letters per line, crowding and irregular progression make it less reproducible than LogMAR, and it is unreliable in children, poor English literacy or non-verbal patients (use Kay pictures, Tumbling-E or LogMAR).
A normal VA does not exclude serious disease — peripheral retinal detachment, early glaucoma or a small field defect can spare the fovea; always assess fields, pupils and fundus too.
Dilating drops (tropicamide) aid fundal slit-lamp views but blur vision for hours (warn re driving) and can precipitate angle closure in a predisposed narrow-angle eye.
🚩 Do NOT dilate a patient with a red, painful eye, a hazy cornea and a fixed mid-dilated pupil — suspected acute angle-closure glaucoma. Dilation worsens the block; this is a sight-threatening emergency needing same-day ophthalmology referral and IOP-lowering treatment.
🎓 The pinhole is your bedside refractionist: if VA of 6/24 improves to 6/9 through a pinhole, the problem is glasses, not the retina or optic nerve. Any acuity worse than 6/60 should be documented as CF / HM / PL — never just “can't read the chart”.

Fundoscopy is the direct visualisation of the retina, optic disc, macula and retinal vessels through the pupil, most commonly using a direct ophthalmoscope; the red reflex is the orange-red glow of light reflected off the vascularised retina and is the fastest bedside screen for any opacity in the visual axis. Together they let you assess the optic nerve head (colour, margins, cup:disc ratio), the retinal vasculature and macula, and — via the red reflex — detect sight- and life-threatening opacities such as cataract, vitreous haemorrhage and retinoblastoma. Dilating the pupil with tropicamide 1% (± phenylephrine 2.5%) dramatically widens the view and is standard for a proper dilated fundal examination.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Fundoscopy assesses the only part of the CNS and microvasculature visible directly. The direct ophthalmoscope projects light through the pupil and gives a highly magnified (×15), upright, but narrow monocular field. The red reflex works on the same principle: light entering a clear media and healthy retina returns as a uniform red-orange glow — any opacity between cornea and retina blocks or distorts it.

🔬Optic disc
Glaucoma, papilloedema, optic atrophy, disc swelling
🩸Vessels
Diabetic & hypertensive retinopathy, vessel occlusion
🎯Macula
Age-related macular degeneration, diabetic maculopathy
👶Red reflex
Neonatal screen for cataract & retinoblastoma
Every newborn and 6-week baby check must include a red reflex assessment (NIPE screening).
Fundoscopy is mandatory in headache with visual symptoms, suspected raised ICP, diabetes and hypertension review, and sudden visual loss.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Darken the room to encourage natural pupil dilation. For a full dilated exam instil tropicamide 1% (short-acting mydriatic; onset ~15-20 min, lasts 4-6 h), adding phenylephrine 2.5% if a wider pupil is needed. Ask the patient to fixate on a distant target and to keep looking straight ahead even when your head blocks their view.

Same-same rule: examine the patient's RIGHT eye with YOUR right eye holding the scope in your RIGHT hand; swap for the left.
Set the lens dial to 0 (or your own refractive correction), start at arm's length ~15° temporal to catch the red reflex, then move in close.
Follow a vessel back to the optic disc, examine disc → four vascular arcades → macula last (ask patient to look directly at the light).
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ophthalmic view / finding (e.g. a normal fundus showing a well-defined pink optic disc with cup:disc ~0.3, and a bright uniform red reflex in both eyes on Bruckner test).

A normal disc is round/oval, pink-orange with a paler central cup, sharp margins and a cup:disc ratio around 0.3. A normal red reflex is bright, uniform and symmetrical (equal brightness/colour between eyes on the Bruckner test).

3INTERPRETATION
Cup:disc ratio ≥ 0.6 or asymmetry > 0.2→Glaucomatous optic neuropathy — refer
Blurred disc margins, no cup, engorged veins→Papilloedema — raised ICP until proven otherwise
Pale, well-defined disc→Optic atrophy
Dot-blot haemorrhages, microaneurysms, exudates→Diabetic retinopathy
AV nipping, flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots→Hypertensive retinopathy
White reflex (leukocoria)→Retinoblastoma or congenital cataract — urgent referral
Absent / dull red reflex in an adult→Cataract or vitreous haemorrhage
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
Direct ophthalmoscopy has a narrow field and gives NO stereopsis — peripheral retinal detachments and tears are easily missed; it does not replace slit-lamp indirect examination.
An undilated pupil, media opacity or poor patient fixation severely limits the view; small pupils in the elderly are a common cause of a "failed" exam.
Tropicamide causes transient blurred vision and photophobia — warn against driving until it wears off.
A slightly dull red reflex can be normal in darkly pigmented fundi; compare the two eyes for asymmetry rather than judging one in isolation.
🚩 Do NOT dilate a shallow anterior chamber or an eye with suspected acute angle-closure glaucoma (painful red eye, haloes, fixed mid-dilated pupil, nausea) — mydriatics can precipitate an acute pressure spike. Acute angle closure is a sight-threatening emergency needing same-day ophthalmology referral.
🎓 In any neonate a WHITE red reflex (leukocoria) is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise and warrants urgent same-day referral — it is life-threatening, not just sight-threatening. Always check the red reflex in BOTH eyes and compare them.

Tonometry measures the intraocular pressure (IOP) — the fluid pressure inside the eye generated by the balance between aqueous humour production (ciliary body) and drainage (trabecular meshwork). It is the single most important modifiable risk factor in glaucoma. Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT), performed at the slit-lamp, is the gold-standard technique and works on the Imbert–Fick principle: the force needed to flatten (applanate) a fixed 3.06 mm diameter of cornea is directly proportional to the IOP.

1Indication & principle

IOP measurement is central to diagnosing and monitoring glaucoma and ocular hypertension, assessing a red painful eye, and evaluating trauma or post-operative eyes. GAT is preferred because at the standardised 3.06 mm applanation diameter the corneal rigidity and tear-film surface tension roughly cancel out, so the flattening force reads directly as pressure.

🔬Goldmann (GAT)
Slit-lamp mounted; gold standard; uses fluorescein + anaesthetic
💨Non-contact (air-puff)
No anaesthetic; screening/optometry; less accurate at extremes
📍iCare rebound
Handheld probe; no anaesthetic; useful in children & bedside
🖊️Tono-Pen
Portable applanation; useful with scarred/irregular corneas
2How it is performed (GAT)
Instil topical anaesthetic (e.g. proxymetacaine/tetracaine) combined with fluorescein — often via a Fluoret strip or combined amethocaine-fluorescein drop.
Seat the patient at the slit-lamp, chin on rest, and select the cobalt blue filter. The prism head is mounted on the biomicroscope.
Advance the prism to just touch the corneal apex; two fluorescein-stained semicircles (mires) appear.
Turn the calibrated dial until the inner edges of the two semicircles just touch, forming an S-shape. The dial reading × 10 gives the IOP in mmHg.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ophthalmic view / finding (e.g. the two blue-green fluorescein mires viewed through the cobalt filter at correct end-point, with inner edges just apposed).

A normal end-point is stable with gentle pulsatile movement of the mires from ocular pulse. Excessively thick mires mean too much fluorescein or too much pressure applied.

3Interpretation & thresholds

Normal IOP is approximately 10–21 mmHg (mean ~15–16 mmHg), with slight diurnal variation (typically higher in the morning).

IOP 10–21 mmHg→Statistically normal range
IOP >21 mmHg, normal disc & fields→Ocular hypertension — a glaucoma risk factor; monitor
Raised IOP + optic disc cupping + VF loss→Primary open-angle glaucoma
Glaucomatous damage with IOP ≤21 mmHg→Normal-tension glaucoma
IOP >40–50 mmHg, red painful eye→Acute angle-closure glaucoma — emergency
Very low IOP (hypotony, <6 mmHg)→Wound leak, over-filtration, or globe rupture

NICE thresholds for referral in ocular hypertension centre on IOP together with central corneal thickness (CCT) and age, since higher IOP with a thinner cornea carries greater risk.

4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Central corneal thickness (CCT): a thin cornea underestimates true IOP and a thick cornea overestimates it — GAT is calibrated to a CCT of ~520 µm.
Corneal factors: scarring, oedema, high astigmatism (>3 D) and previous refractive surgery (e.g. LASIK, which thins the cornea) reduce accuracy.
Technique errors: excess fluorescein gives falsely high readings; too little gives falsely low; patient breath-holding, tight collars or Valsalva transiently raise IOP.
Infection control & contact risk: GAT touches the cornea, so requires anaesthetic and a disinfected/disposable prism; avoid in active corneal infection or after recent surgery.
🚩 A markedly raised IOP (often >40–50 mmHg) with a red, painful eye, hazy cornea, fixed mid-dilated pupil and haloes around lights is acute angle-closure glaucoma — a sight-threatening emergency needing same-day ophthalmology referral. Do NOT pharmacologically dilate a suspected angle-closure eye, as this can precipitate or worsen the attack.
🎓 Remember the Imbert–Fick shortcut: the Goldmann dial reading is in grams and you simply multiply by 10 to get mmHg (e.g. a dial reading of 1.6 = 16 mmHg). Always interpret IOP alongside CCT — a “normal” reading over a thin cornea may mask true elevation.

Gonioscopy is the slit-lamp examination of the iridocorneal (drainage) angle using a mirrored contact goniolens. Because the cornea-air interface causes total internal reflection, light from the angle recess never escapes to the examiner's eye, so the angle cannot be seen directly at the slit-lamp; a goniolens overcomes this and lets you grade the angle open versus narrow/closed. It is the reference-standard test for classifying glaucoma — distinguishing primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) from angle-closure — and for deciding whether a patient needs prophylactic laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI).

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Every patient with suspected or established glaucoma, raised intraocular pressure (IOP), a shallow anterior chamber, or symptoms of intermittent angle closure (haloes, brow-ache) should have gonioscopy. It answers one central question: is the trabecular meshwork open and visible, or is it occluded by iris?

The optical problem: at the cornea-air interface, light reflected from the angle exceeds the critical angle and undergoes total internal reflection, so the recess is invisible on routine slit-lamp view.
The solution: a goniolens (with coupling fluid) replaces the cornea-air interface with a lens-fluid interface, eliminating total internal reflection; mirrors then reflect the angle image back to the examiner.
🔬Schwalbe's line
Termination of Descemet's membrane; the anterior-most landmark
🔬Trabecular meshwork
The functional drainage tissue; often pigmented posteriorly
🔬Scleral spur
White band; key reference — if visible the angle is open
🔬Ciliary body band
Grey-brown band posterior to spur; deepest structure seen

Remember the sequence anterior→posterior as "A Sad Trabecular Sees Ciliary": Anterior chamber, Schwalbe's line, Trabecular meshwork, Scleral spur, Ciliary body band.

2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Gonioscopy is done at the slit-lamp with the patient seated and comfortable. Key steps:

Instil topical anaesthetic (e.g. proxymetacaine/tetracaine). Crucially, perform gonioscopy before dilating drops so the angle is assessed in its natural state.
Apply a coupling agent to the goniolens face if using an indirect (Goldmann-type, mirrored) lens; a direct lens (Koeppe) is used supine, mainly in theatre/EUA.
Use a short, narrow, bright slit beam offset from the mirror. Keep the beam off the pupil — light-induced constriction artificially deepens the angle and can mask an occludable angle.
Rotate the mirror to view all four quadrants. Indentation (dynamic) gonioscopy with a small-footplate lens (e.g. Zeiss/Sussman four-mirror) presses on the cornea to distinguish appositional from synechial (permanent) closure.
📷 Image placeholder — goniophotograph of an open angle showing, from cornea inward, Schwalbe's line, pigmented trabecular meshwork, white scleral spur and the ciliary body band.
3INTERPRETATION — OPEN vs CLOSED

Grade each quadrant by the deepest structure visible and by the angular width. The Shaffer grade estimates the angle between iris and trabecular meshwork; the simplest rule of thumb is whether the scleral spur can be seen.

Ciliary body band clearly visible (Shaffer 4, ~35–45°)→Wide open angle — closure not possible
Scleral spur visible (Shaffer 3, ~20–35°)→Open angle — closure not possible
Only trabecular meshwork seen (Shaffer 2, ~20°)→Moderately narrow — closure possible
Only Schwalbe's line / anterior meshwork (Shaffer 1, ~10°)→Very narrow — closure probable; consider LPI
No angle structures visible (Shaffer 0, iridocorneal contact)→Closed angle — angle-closure present
Peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) on indentation→Chronic/synechial closure — iris permanently adherent
Heavy TM pigment / a Sampaolesi line→Suggests pigment dispersion or pseudoexfoliation
Abnormal vessels crossing the scleral spur→Neovascularisation (rubeosis) — ischaemic retina
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
Light artefact: a bright beam on the pupil constricts the iris and falsely opens a narrow angle — always keep the beam off the pupil and examine in a dim room.
Over-indentation: pressing too hard with a four-mirror lens creates corneal folds and artificially widens the angle, masking appositional closure.
Operator dependence: results vary with examiner experience; imaging adjuncts (anterior-segment OCT, UBM) complement but do not replace gonioscopy, which remains the reference standard.
Missed pathology: a normal-looking angle can still hide low-grade PAS or subtle neovascularisation — always view all four quadrants.
🚩 In suspected acute angle-closure glaucoma (painful red eye, fixed mid-dilated pupil, haloes, hazy cornea, very high IOP) do NOT instil mydriatic/dilating drops — dilation can precipitate or worsen closure. This is a sight-threatening emergency needing immediate IOP-lowering treatment and urgent same-day ophthalmology referral.
🎓 The single fastest exam answer: if you can see the scleral spur, the angle is open. The scleral spur is the pivotal landmark separating open (spur/ciliary band visible) from occludable (spur hidden) angles.

The swinging-light test is a bedside examination that detects a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), also called a Marcus Gunn pupil. A bright light is swung rhythmically from one eye to the other; the test compares the strength of the light signal reaching the brain through each optic nerve (CN II). A RAPD is present when the affected pupil paradoxically dilates as the light swings onto it, revealing a lesion of the retina or optic nerve on that side. It is a purely afferent and relative test — it needs asymmetry between the two eyes and is unaffected by media opacity such as cataract or by refractive error.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Both pupils constrict equally to light shone in either eye because the pupillary light reflex has a consensual arm: afferent signals from one optic nerve drive constriction of both pupils via the pretectal nuclei. If one optic nerve conducts less well than the other, swinging the light to the weaker side produces less total constrictor drive, so both pupils drift open — seen as apparent dilation of the illuminated eye.

🔬Afferent limb
Retina → optic nerve (CN II) — the pathway being tested
⚖️Relative
Compares the two eyes; needs asymmetry to show up
🩺Objective
Cannot be faked; independent of patient-reported vision
👁️Localises
Pinpoints unilateral/asymmetric optic nerve or retinal disease
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Dim the room and ask the patient to fixate on a distant target to relax accommodation. Use a bright focused light (pen-torch or indirect ophthalmoscope bulb).

Shine the light into one eye for 2–3 seconds and watch the direct response, then swing briskly across the bridge of the nose to the other eye.
Hold on each eye for the same short interval and swing back and forth several times, watching the pupil of the eye into which the light has just moved.
Normal: each pupil either stays constricted or shows a tiny escape then re-constriction, symmetrically on both sides.
Keep the light at the same angle and brightness for each eye — unequal illumination fabricates a false defect.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ophthalmic view / finding (e.g. the affected pupil dilating as the swung light reaches it, versus symmetric constriction in a normal test).
3INTERPRETATION

A RAPD is graded by the degree and speed of dilation of the affected pupil. The side that dilates is the abnormal (afferent) side.

Affected pupil DILATES as light swings to it→Positive RAPD — optic nerve/retinal lesion that side
Optic neuritis (e.g. demyelination)→Classic cause of a unilateral RAPD, often with pain on eye movement
Ischaemic optic neuropathy / CRAO→RAPD with sudden painless visual loss
Large retinal detachment→RAPD proportional to extent of retina involved
Dense asymmetric glaucoma→RAPD on the more advanced side
Cataract / refractive error→NO RAPD — media opacity does not reduce afferent conduction
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
The test only works if disease is asymmetric: bilateral symmetric optic neuropathy gives no RAPD despite poor vision in both eyes.
An efferent problem (e.g. a fixed dilated pupil from a third-nerve palsy or previous surgery) can obscure interpretation — watch the reactive pupil, or the consensual response in the abnormal eye.
Unequal light intensity, an inattentive patient, or accommodation to a near target can produce a false or missed defect.
A RAPD does not localise to a single diagnosis — it flags afferent pathology needing further assessment (fundoscopy, fields, imaging).
🚩 A new RAPD signals significant optic nerve or retinal disease and is never normal — combined with sudden visual loss it demands urgent ophthalmology referral (e.g. to exclude CRAO or giant cell arteritis).
🎓 Remember the paradox: in a RAPD the affected pupil dilates to light. The eye that gets bigger when you shine the torch on it is the sick one — and because both pupils always move together, you can still detect it even if the abnormal pupil is pharmacologically or structurally fixed by watching the healthy fellow pupil.

Fluorescein staining is a rapid bedside dye test that reveals breaches in the corneal (and conjunctival) epithelium. Topical fluorescein — a 2% drop or a moistened impregnated strip — pools in and binds to areas of epithelial loss where the underlying stroma is exposed. Viewed under cobalt-blue light it fluoresces bright green, so abrasions, ulcers and the branching dendrite of herpes simplex keratitis stand out against an otherwise dark, intact surface. It is one of the highest-yield tests in acute ophthalmology: cheap, instant, and often the single investigation that decides diagnosis and disposition.

1Indication & principle

Fluorescein is a water-soluble dye that does not penetrate an intact, lipid-rich epithelium but is taken up wherever epithelial cells are missing and the hydrophilic stroma is bare. Under cobalt-blue (or a Wood's/blue-light) illumination it emits green light, mapping the exact size and pattern of any epithelial defect. Use it whenever a patient presents with a red, painful, watering or photophobic eye, a foreign-body sensation, or after suspected trauma or contact-lens misuse.

🩹Corneal abrasion
Traumatic epithelial scratch — well-defined staining area
🦠Bacterial ulcer
Epithelial defect over a white stromal infiltrate
🌿HSV dendrite
Branching linear ulcer with terminal bulbs — herpes simplex
💧Seidel-positive leak
Streaming dilution of dye — full-thickness aqueous leak
2How it is performed
Instil a drop of topical anaesthetic (e.g. proxymetacaine) first if the eye is too painful to open — this also improves patient cooperation.
Moisten a fluorescein strip with saline (or use a combined fluorescein/anaesthetic drop) and touch it gently to the inferior tarsal conjunctiva; ask the patient to blink to spread the dye across the tear film.
Examine under cobalt-blue light — ideally the slit lamp, but a blue-light pen torch or the blue filter of a direct ophthalmoscope will do at the bedside.
A normal cornea shows a smooth even green tear film with NO focal uptake; any bright green patch that persists after a blink indicates epithelial loss.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the cobalt-blue slit-lamp view of a branching green dendritic ulcer with terminal end-bulbs on the corneal surface.
3Interpretation of patterns
Fine scattered punctate dots (inferior/interpalpebral)→Punctate epithelial erosions — dry eye, exposure or toxicity
Single well-demarcated stained area, no infiltrate→Corneal abrasion — often traumatic or foreign-body related
Branching linear ulcer with terminal end-bulbs→Dendritic ulcer of HSV keratitis — start topical aciclovir
Broad amoeboid ('map-like') defect→Geographic ulcer — advanced/steroid-modified HSV
Round epithelial defect over a white/grey stromal opacity→Microbial (bacterial) keratitis — sight-threatening, needs corneal scrape
Vertical linear scratches (fine parallel lines) high on cornea→Sub-tarsal foreign body — evert the upper lid
Bright stream of dye diluting a dark rivulet (Seidel test)→Aqueous leak from a perforation — ophthalmic emergency
4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Soft contact lenses absorb fluorescein and stain permanently — always remove lenses before instilling dye.
Pooling of dye in tear-film irregularities, mucus or a slightly heaped edge can mimic uptake; re-check after a blink and correlate with symptoms.
A subtle dendrite can be missed if you rely on a dim pen-torch blue filter — use the slit lamp whenever possible.
Stain reveals the epithelial defect but NOT depth or infiltrate — always assess the stroma and anterior chamber for hypopyon.
🚩 A branching dendritic ulcer means HSV epithelial keratitis — do NOT prescribe topical corticosteroids alone, as they promote viral replication and can convert a dendrite into a sight-threatening geographic ulcer. A contact-lens wearer with a stromal infiltrate and epithelial defect needs urgent same-day ophthalmology referral for corneal scrape/microbiology and intensive topical antibiotics (Pseudomonas cover).
🎓 In the exam, the classic pairing to recall is: dendrite = herpes simplex (aciclovir, avoid steroids), while a Seidel-positive stream = globe perforation (shield the eye, keep nil-by-mouth, urgent surgical review). Terminal end-bulbs distinguish an HSV dendrite from the pseudodendrites of herpes zoster, which lack them and stain poorly.
OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging & Visual Fields:
Visual field testing (perimetry) maps the extent of vision seen by each eye while it fixates straight ahead. Because the retinal nerve fibres, chiasm and post-chiasmal pathways carry information in a strict retinotopic order, the shape and laterality of a field defect localises the lesion along the visual pathway. It is the core investigation for diagnosing and monitoring glaucoma and for detecting neurological compression such as a pituitary tumour.

1Indication & principle

Perimetry quantifies retinal sensitivity across the visual field. A monocular defect localises to the retina or optic nerve (in front of the chiasm); a binocular defect respecting the vertical midline localises to the chiasm or behind it.

🔬Confrontation
Bedside screen comparing patient's field to examiner's
🖥️Humphrey
Automated static perimetry; standard for glaucoma
🎯Goldmann
Kinetic perimetry mapping isopters; good for large defects
📍Amsler grid
Central 10° screen for macular distortion/scotoma
2How it is performed

For confrontation, sit about 1 metre facing the patient at eye level. Test one eye at a time: the patient covers the opposite eye and fixates on your nose while you cover your own opposing eye. Bring a target (moving fingers or a red pin) inward from the periphery in each of the four quadrants, comparing when the patient sees it against your own field. A red target detects subtle desaturation and central scotomata.

Static perimetry presents stationary lights of varying brightness at fixed points; the patient presses a button when a spot is seen.
Kinetic perimetry moves a target of fixed size/brightness inward until seen, tracing isopters of equal sensitivity.
A normal monocular field extends roughly 60° nasally/superiorly, 90° temporally and 70° inferiorly, with a physiological blind spot ~15° temporal to fixation.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ophthalmic view / finding (e.g. a Humphrey grey-scale printout showing a bitemporal hemianopia respecting the vertical midline).
3Interpretation of defect patterns

Read the pattern first, then the laterality. Defects that respect the vertical midline are chiasmal or post-chiasmal; those respecting the horizontal midline are typically optic nerve/retinal (glaucoma, ischaemia).

Central scotoma (monocular)→Macular disease or optic neuropathy (e.g. optic neuritis)
Arcuate scotoma / nasal step→Glaucomatous retinal nerve fibre loss
Altitudinal defect (respects horizontal)→Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy / retinal vascular occlusion
Bitemporal hemianopia→Optic chiasm compression (pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma)
Homonymous hemianopia→Contralateral post-chiasmal lesion (tract, radiation, occipital cortex)
Homonymous with macular sparing→Occipital (cortical) lesion; dual blood supply spares the macula
Superior quadrantanopia (“pie in the sky”)→Temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) lesion
4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Automated perimetry is subjective and effort-dependent; fatigue, poor fixation and learning effects reduce reliability. Check reliability indices (fixation losses, false positives/negatives).
Ptosis, a high nasal bridge, uncorrected refractive error or small pupils produce artefactual defects that mimic disease.
Confrontation is insensitive to early or subtle loss and may entirely miss shallow glaucomatous defects — a normal confrontation does not exclude pathology.
🚩 A new bitemporal hemianopia suggests chiasmal compression (often a pituitary tumour) and warrants urgent neuroimaging; a sudden homonymous hemianopia may signify an occipital stroke — arrange emergency assessment rather than reassurance.
🎓 Localisation rule: monocular field loss is pre-chiasmal (eye/optic nerve), while any defect respecting the vertical midline is at or behind the chiasm. The more congruous (symmetrical between the two eyes) a homonymous defect, the more posterior the lesion.

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is a rapid, non-invasive, non-contact 'optical biopsy' of the retina that uses low-coherence interferometry to build micron-resolution, cross-sectional images of the retinal layers. Analogous to B-scan ultrasound but using light rather than sound, it resolves the neurosensory retina into its constituent layers, letting clinicians detect fluid, structural distortion and layer thinning that are invisible on standard fundoscopy. It anchors two everyday tasks: macular OCT for macular disease (wet AMD, diabetic macular oedema) and RNFL/disc OCT for glaucoma diagnosis and monitoring.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Near-infrared light is split into a reference and a sample beam; light back-scattered from retinal layers is recombined and the interference pattern is used to map tissue reflectivity against depth (A-scan), which are stacked into a 2D cross-section (B-scan). Modern spectral-domain (SD-OCT) devices achieve axial resolution of roughly 5–7 micrometres, fast enough to avoid motion artefact and detect tiny volumes of fluid.

🔬Wet AMD
Detect intraretinal/subretinal fluid to start and monitor anti-VEGF
🩸Diabetic macular oedema
Quantify central retinal thickness to guide treatment
🕳️Macular hole / ERM
Confirm full-thickness hole or epiretinal membrane before surgery
👁️Glaucoma
Measure RNFL and ganglion cell layer thinning over time
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

The seated patient rests on a chin-and-forehead rest and fixates on an internal target while the operator focuses the beam and captures a volume scan in seconds. No dye or contact is needed, and it can usually be done through an undilated pupil, though dilation improves image quality with media opacity or small pupils. Two protocols dominate:

Macular cube — a raster over the fovea producing B-scans plus a colour-coded thickness map; a normal fovea shows the characteristic central foveal pit with smooth, continuous layers and an intact ellipsoid zone.
RNFL / optic disc scan — a circular or cube scan around the disc measuring peripapillary RNFL thickness, cup:disc ratio and rim area, compared against a normative database and colour-coded green (normal), yellow (borderline) or red (outside normal limits).
📷 Image placeholder — macular OCT B-scan showing the normal foveal pit with intact layers alongside a scan with cystoid intraretinal fluid and subretinal fluid in wet AMD.
3INTERPRETATION
Intraretinal / subretinal fluid on macular OCT→Active exudative (wet) AMD or diabetic macular oedema — indication for anti-VEGF
Drusen (sub-RPE deposits), preserved layers, no fluid→Dry AMD — monitor, no anti-VEGF
Full-thickness foveal defect with edge cuffing→Full-thickness macular hole — consider vitrectomy
Peripapillary RNFL below normative limits (red sector)→Glaucomatous nerve fibre loss — correlate with disc and visual fields
Cup:disc ratio ≥ 0.7 with thinning inferior/superior rim→Suspicious for glaucomatous optic neuropathy
Progressive RNFL thinning on serial scans→Disease progression — escalate glaucoma therapy
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
Media opacity (dense cataract, vitreous haemorrhage) and poor fixation degrade image quality and cause segmentation errors that misread thickness.
The normative database assumes average axial length — high myopes and large or tilted discs generate false 'red' RNFL readings (red-disease), while very thick tissue can mask early loss (green-disease).
OCT shows structure, not perfusion or function — it does not replace fundus fluorescein angiography for leakage or visual fields for functional glaucoma damage.
🚩 OCT is an adjunct, not a substitute for clinical assessment: a normal macular OCT does not exclude sight-threatening pathology such as an ischaemic central retinal artery occlusion or a retinal detachment outside the scanned area, and painful red eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil suggesting acute angle-closure needs urgent referral and IOP measurement, not reassurance from imaging.
🎓 High yield: fluid on macular OCT is the trigger and treatment target for anti-VEGF in wet AMD and DMO — a 'dry' macula after injections signals disease control, while new or persistent fluid drives re-treatment.

Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) is a dynamic imaging test in which sodium fluorescein dye is injected intravenously and a rapid sequence of fundus photographs captures the dye transiting the retinal and choroidal circulation. It maps perfusion, leakage, ischaemia and neovascularisation over successive phases (arterial, arteriovenous, venous and late), turning invisible vascular pathology into a pattern of bright (hyperfluorescent) and dark (hypofluorescent) areas.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Fluorescein is a small water-soluble molecule that absorbs blue light (~490 nm) and emits green (~530 nm). It is largely confined within normal retinal vessels because tight junctions of the inner blood–retinal barrier (retinal endothelium) and outer barrier (retinal pigment epithelium, RPE) hold it in. Wherever these barriers break down, dye escapes and lights up; wherever vessels are blocked or non-perfused, the background stays dark.

🩸Diabetic retinopathy
Maps capillary non-perfusion, microaneurysm leakage & new vessels to guide laser
🔴Vein / artery occlusion
Distinguishes ischaemic from non-ischaemic RVO; delayed filling in CRAO
💧Wet AMD / CNV
Identifies choroidal neovascular membrane and its leakage pattern
🔥Retinal vasculitis
Vessel-wall staining & leakage in uveitis, sarcoid, Behçet
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

The pupils are dilated (e.g. tropicamide ± phenylephrine) and consent is taken, including a check for previous dye reactions and renal/pregnancy status. Resuscitation facilities must be immediately available.

A baseline colour and red-free (green-filtered) fundus image is taken first.
Sodium fluorescein (usually 5 mL of 10%, or 2–3 mL of 20%) is injected rapidly into an antecubital vein.
A timer starts at injection; rapid serial photographs use a blue excitation filter and a yellow-green barrier filter.
Late images are taken at ~5–10 minutes to capture staining and leakage.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the fluorescein angiogram phases: early choroidal flush, arterial filling, laminar venous flow, and late-phase leakage/staining.

Normal phases and their approximate timings after injection:

Choroidal flush (~10 s)→Patchy background fill; cilioretinal artery may fill early with choroid
Arterial phase (~10–15 s)→Retinal arterioles fill; veins still dark
Arteriovenous / laminar (~15–20 s)→Full arteries plus early laminar venous flow along vein walls
Venous phase (~20–30 s)→Complete venous filling; a dark foveal avascular zone stands out
Late phase (~5–10 min)→Dye washes out; only abnormal leakage or staining remains bright
3INTERPRETATION

Every abnormality reduces to too much fluorescence (hyperfluorescence) or too little (hypofluorescence), then refined by timing and pattern.

Early hyperfluorescence, no leakage (window defect)→RPE atrophy letting choroidal dye show through (e.g. dry AMD)
Progressive leakage (increasing & blurred over time)→Barrier breakdown — CNV, macular oedema, active new vessels
Focal early hyperfluorescent dots→Microaneurysms in diabetic retinopathy
Staining (fixed, well-demarcated late glow)→Dye held in scar, drusen or sclerotic vessel wall (vasculitis)
Hypofluorescence — blockage→Overlying haemorrhage, exudate or pigment masks normal fill
Hypofluorescence — non-perfusion / filling defect→Capillary dropout (ischaemia) or delayed arterial filling (CRAO)
Large areas of capillary non-perfusion in RVO→Ischaemic subtype — high neovascular risk, close monitoring / laser
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
Nearly all patients get transient yellow discolouration of skin and bright yellow urine for 24–48 h — warn them in advance.
Nausea and vomiting are common in the first minute; vasovagal episodes and skin extravasation (painful) also occur.
Rarely, severe reactions occur: urticaria, bronchospasm and true anaphylaxis — hence resuscitation equipment must be to hand.
Fluorescein is renally excreted; use caution and clear consent in significant renal impairment, and generally avoid in pregnancy unless essential.
FFA images the retinal circulation well but is poor for deep choroidal detail — indocyanine green (ICG) angiography is preferred there.
Media opacity (dense cataract, vitreous haemorrhage) and poor pupil dilation degrade image quality.
🚩 Fluorescein can cause anaphylaxis, so FFA must only be performed where resuscitation facilities and trained staff are immediately available. Always ask about prior dye reactions and asthma, obtain informed consent, and counsel patients about transient yellow skin and urine. Warn diabetics that fluorescein can interfere with capillary glucose readings for ~1 day.
🎓 Learn the reciprocal pair: a window defect is bright early and fades as dye clears (RPE atrophy exposing choroid), whereas leakage starts subtle and grows brighter and blurrier with time (active CNV/oedema). Timing distinguishes them — and only leakage flags treatable wet disease.

The Amsler grid is a hand-held card of straight horizontal and vertical lines forming small squares, with a central fixation dot. Tested one eye at a time (the other covered), in reading glasses, held at ~30 cm under good lighting, it maps the central ~10° of the visual field (the macula). It is a sensitive early-warning tool for macular dysfunction: patients report metamorphopsia (wavy, bent or distorted lines) or a central scotoma (a missing, greyed or blurred patch), most importantly to catch conversion of dry to wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

1Indication & principle

The grid projects onto the macula when the eye fixates the central dot. Because photoreceptors are packed densely at the fovea, a small area of macular pathology produces a disproportionate, easily perceived distortion. Displacement or swelling of photoreceptors (by subretinal fluid, oedema or a hole) makes straight lines appear wavy; loss of function makes squares disappear.

🔬Wet AMD monitoring
Home use in dry AMD; new distortion flags choroidal neovascularisation
💧Macular oedema
Diabetic maculopathy, retinal vein occlusion, post-op CMO
🕳️Macular hole / pucker
Central scotoma or metamorphopsia from a full-thickness hole or epiretinal membrane
💊Drug toxicity
Screening adjunct for hydroxychloroquine maculopathy
2How it is performed
Wear your usual reading glasses and hold the grid at a comfortable reading distance (~30 cm) in good, even light.
Cover one eye. With the open eye, look steadily at the central dot and keep fixating it throughout — do not let the gaze wander over the grid.
While staring at the dot, notice the surrounding squares: are all four corners visible, are the lines straight and unbroken, are any areas missing, blurred, grey or wavy?
Repeat with the other eye. No dilating drops or dyes are needed — it is a purely subjective functional test done monocularly.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ophthalmic view / finding (a normal Amsler grid of straight squares beside an abnormal grid showing wavy central lines and a dark central scotoma).

Normal result: the central dot is seen, the grid fills the field, all lines are straight and parallel, all squares are equal, and there are no missing, wavy or blurred areas.

3Interpretation
Wavy / bent / distorted lines (metamorphopsia)→Macular distortion from subretinal fluid or oedema — suspect wet AMD, arrange urgent OCT
Central or paracentral missing patch (scotoma)→Loss of macular function — macular hole, geographic atrophy or dense oedema
New change compared with the patient's baseline→Conversion event until proven otherwise — prompts same-week macula clinic review
Blurred or greyed squares in one region→Localised macular oedema or serous elevation — correlate with OCT
Straight lines, intact grid, both eyes→Reassuring — continue routine monitoring, retest if symptoms change

The key clinical value is change over time: a stable dry-AMD patient given a grid for the fridge or bathroom mirror tests weekly, so any newly appearing distortion is reported early, within the window where anti-VEGF therapy best preserves vision.

4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Subjective & fixation-dependent: results rely on the patient maintaining central fixation and reporting honestly; poor understanding gives false results.
Perceptual filling-in: the brain can "complete" a scotoma, so small defects may be missed — a normal grid does not exclude macular disease.
Must wear reading correction: uncorrected refractive error or media opacity (cataract) blurs the grid and mimics or masks pathology.
Not a substitute for imaging: it detects and monitors but does not diagnose — abnormalities need OCT ± fundus examination to confirm.
🚩 A patient with known dry AMD who reports new distortion or a new central scotoma on their Amsler grid must be treated as possible conversion to wet AMD and referred for urgent (typically within one week) macular assessment and OCT — delay risks irreversible sight loss from untreated choroidal neovascularisation.
🎓 High-yield: metamorphopsia (wavy lines on the Amsler grid) localises pathology to the macula, not the optic nerve or media — a distortion described as "the door frame looks bent" is a classic AMD presenting complaint.

B-scan ocular ultrasound is a bedside, radiation-free imaging technique that uses high-frequency sound waves (typically 10–20 MHz) to produce a two-dimensional cross-sectional image of the globe and orbit. Its cardinal role is to visualise the posterior segment when the direct view is blocked by opaque ocular media — a dense cataract, vitreous haemorrhage, or hyphaema — and to characterise intraocular and orbital masses. When you cannot see in, B-scan tells you what is happening behind the opaque media.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

A B-scan (brightness-mode) probe emits ultrasound pulses and reconstructs the returning echoes into a grey-scale sagittal or transverse section. Tissue interfaces of differing acoustic impedance (retina, vitreous, sclera, tumour) reflect sound to varying degrees, giving each structure a characteristic reflectivity. It is quick, non-invasive, involves no ionising radiation, and can be performed at the bedside or in clinic.

🔬Opaque media
Dense cataract, vitreous haemorrhage or hyphaema obscuring fundoscopy
🩸Suspected RD
Sudden flashes/floaters/field loss with no fundal view
🎯Intraocular mass
Characterise suspected melanoma, metastasis or retinoblastoma calcification
💧Posterior scleritis
Look for fluid in Tenon's space (the T-sign)
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

The patient reclines with eyes gently closed. Topical coupling gel is applied to the closed lid (a sterile approach directly on the globe with anaesthetic drops is used if needed). The probe is placed on the lid and the operator asks the patient to move the eye in different directions to perform kinetic (dynamic) scanning — watching how structures move helps distinguish a mobile membrane from a fixed one. Transverse and longitudinal sweeps survey the whole posterior segment. No pupil dilation is required, which is a key advantage when dilation is contraindicated.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the B-scan appearance: a bright, folded membrane tethered at the optic disc (funnel-shaped retinal detachment) versus low-reflective mobile dots of vitreous haemorrhage.
A normal B-scan shows a clear, acoustically empty (anechoic) vitreous cavity with a smooth concave posterior wall.
Dynamic scanning (after-movement) is essential to grade the mobility of any membrane seen.
3INTERPRETATION — KEY FINDINGS

Interpretation rests on the reflectivity, shape, attachment and mobility of echoes within the vitreous cavity.

Bright, thick membrane tethered to the optic disc, funnel/V-shaped, limited after-movement→Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
Low-to-medium reflective mobile dots/clumps swirling freely in vitreous→Vitreous haemorrhage
Thin, highly mobile membrane NOT attached at the disc, marked after-movement→Posterior vitreous detachment
Dome- or collar-stud/mushroom-shaped solid mass with low internal reflectivity & acoustic hollowing→Choroidal melanoma
Highly reflective mass with acoustic shadowing (calcification) in a child→Retinoblastoma
Fluid in Tenon's space tracking around the optic nerve (T-sign) with thickened sclera→Posterior scleritis
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY

B-scan is highly operator-dependent, and subtle findings can be missed by the inexperienced. Excessive probe pressure can distort the globe and create artefact, and a fresh mild vitreous haemorrhage may be missed at low gain — scanning at high gain first, then reducing it, avoids overlooking low-reflective pathology. It gives no functional information (no acuity or field) and cannot reliably assess the macula through very dense opacity.

A total retinal detachment can mimic, and be mimicked by, dense vitreous membranes — disc attachment and mobility are the discriminators.
Do NOT apply a probe directly onto the globe when an open globe / ruptured globe is suspected — pressure risks extrusion of intraocular contents.
🚩 Never place ultrasound pressure on an eye with a suspected open (ruptured) globe or penetrating injury — this can express intraocular contents and cause devastating, irreversible sight loss. Protect the eye with a shield and obtain urgent ophthalmology and imaging (CT) instead.
🎓 The T-sign — a right-angled fluid collection where the anechoic gap in Tenon's space meets the optic nerve shadow — is the classic B-scan sign of posterior scleritis, a high-yield answer for a painful red eye with proptosis and a normal-looking fundus.

Diabetic Retinal Screening uses digital retinal photography to detect diabetic retinopathy in its asymptomatic stage, before sight is threatened. The UK national Diabetic Eye Screening Programme (DESP) invites every person with diabetes aged ≥12 for annual dilated fundus photography (two 45° fields per eye), because diabetic retinopathy remains the commonest cause of certifiable blindness in the working-age population — and the early stages produce no symptoms. Systematic screening identifies treatable disease so that timely laser or anti-VEGF therapy can prevent irreversible visual loss.

1Indication & principle

All patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes aged ≥12 are entered onto the screening register and recalled annually. The rationale is that hyperglycaemic microvascular damage progresses silently: microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates and new vessels can be photographed and graded long before the patient notices blurring. Detecting sight-threatening disease early allows intervention while vision is still preservable.

🔬Microaneurysms
Earliest sign; tiny red dots at capillary level
🩸Dot/blot haemorrhages
Intraretinal bleeding from leaky vessels
🟡Hard exudates
Lipid deposits; risk to macula if near fovea
🌱Neovascularisation
Fragile new vessels; proliferative, sight-threatening
2How it is performed

Visual acuity is recorded first. Pupils are dilated with tropicamide 1% (a short-acting mydriatic; phenylephrine may be added) to open the view of the posterior pole and periphery. Using a non-mydriatic or mydriatic digital fundus camera, two fields per eye are captured — one centred on the macula and one on the optic disc — giving standardised, storable images that are graded off-site by trained graders rather than examined live. A normal screen shows a healthy disc, flat macula and clear vessels with no microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates or new vessels.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the fundoscopic screening view: two-field colour photographs showing scattered dot/blot haemorrhages, microaneurysms and hard exudates of background retinopathy versus fragile disc neovascularisation of proliferative disease.
3Interpretation & grading

Each eye is given a retinopathy grade (R) and a maculopathy grade (M). The grade drives the recall interval or referral to the hospital eye service (HES).

R0 — no retinopathy→Routine annual recall
R1 — background (microaneurysms, few haemorrhages/exudates)→Routine annual recall; optimise glycaemic & BP control
R2 — pre-proliferative (venous beading, IRMA, multiple blot haemorrhages)→Refer to hospital eye service
R3 — proliferative (new vessels, vitreous/pre-retinal haemorrhage)→Urgent HES referral for laser (PRP) / anti-VEGF
M1 — maculopathy (exudates/haemorrhage near fovea, macular thickening)→Refer to HES; often OCT and anti-VEGF
R1 and M0 stay in routine annual screening.
R2, R3 and M1 are the referable thresholds that leave the screening pathway for the HES.
4Pitfalls, limitations & safety

Photographs can be ungradable because of cataract, small pupils, poor fixation or media opacity — these patients need slit-lamp biomicroscopy examination rather than being falsely reassured. Screening detects but does not treat, and it can under-call diabetic macular oedema, which is why suspected maculopathy proceeds to OCT. Mydriatic drops blur near vision and preclude driving for several hours, and rarely precipitate acute angle-closure in predisposed eyes.

🚩 Do NOT dilate a patient with a red, painful eye, fixed mid-dilated pupil, haloes and a hazy cornea — this suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma, a sight-threatening emergency needing same-day ophthalmology, not photography. Any patient reporting sudden visual loss, new floaters or a curtain over vision needs urgent referral outside the routine screening pathway.
🎓 Pregnancy accelerates diabetic retinopathy: pre-existing diabetics are screened at booking and again in each trimester, and the standard M/R referral thresholds are applied more readily. Gestational diabetes alone does not require this intensified schedule.
OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscopy Signs & Specia:
Papilloedema is bilateral optic disc swelling caused specifically by raised intracranial pressure (ICP). The term is reserved for disc swelling due to raised ICP; swelling from other causes is called "disc oedema" or "optic disc swelling". Raised cerebrospinal fluid pressure is transmitted along the subarachnoid space surrounding the optic nerve, impairing axoplasmic transport at the optic nerve head. This causes axonal swelling and disc elevation, visible on fundoscopy as blurred, elevated disc margins. Because it signals raised ICP, papilloedema is a red-flag sign that mandates urgent neuroimaging to exclude a mass lesion before any lumbar puncture.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Fundoscopy of the optic disc is performed in any patient with symptoms or signs suggesting raised ICP: new persistent headache (worse on lying flat, waking, straining or coughing), transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, nausea/vomiting, or a sixth-nerve palsy (a false-localising sign). The principle is that CSF surrounds the optic nerve as a continuation of the subarachnoid space, so a rise in ICP is transmitted to the nerve head and blocks orthograde axoplasmic flow, producing axonal swelling and disc elevation.

🧠Space-occupying lesion
Tumour, abscess or haemorrhage raising ICP
⚖️IIH
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension; typically young, obese women
🩸Venous sinus thrombosis
Impaired venous drainage raises ICP
📈Malignant hypertension
Severe accelerated BP with disc swelling
2HOW IT IS ELICITED

Examine in a darkened room with a direct ophthalmoscope, ideally through a pharmacologically dilated pupil (e.g. tropicamide 1%) for the best disc view; modern practice increasingly uses non-mydriatic fundus photography or OCT. Ask the patient to fixate on a distant target and approach temporally at about 15° to bring the disc into view. Assess the disc under four headings: colour, contour (margins), cup, and the vessels. A normal disc has sharp margins (especially nasally, though the nasal edge is normally slightly less crisp), a clear physiological cup, a healthy pink neuroretinal rim and spontaneous venous pulsation visible in most people.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the fundoscopic appearance of a swollen disc: blurred elevated margins, hyperaemic disc, obscured vessels crossing the margin and loss of the cup, with peripapillary Paton's lines.
Colour: hyperaemic (red/pink) disc from capillary dilatation.
Contour: blurred, indistinct disc margins that appear elevated above the retinal plane.
Cup: loss of the physiological cup as swelling fills it in.
Vessels: obscured as they cross the disc margin; loss of spontaneous venous pulsation; in acute cases flame haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots.
3INTERPRETATION

The hallmark is bilateral disc swelling with, characteristically, preserved visual acuity early and an enlarged blind spot on perimetry. Peripheral field constriction and acuity loss are later features of chronic or severe disease. Use the pattern of findings to interpret cause and chronicity.

Bilateral disc swelling + raised ICP symptoms→Papilloedema until proven otherwise; image the brain urgently
Loss of spontaneous venous pulsation→Suggests ICP ≥ ~20 cmH₂O (early, sensitive sign)
Enlarged blind spot, acuity preserved early→Typical of papilloedema; distinguishes it from optic neuritis
Paton's lines (concentric peripapillary retinal folds)→Acute/active disc swelling
Unilateral swollen disc + reduced acuity + RAPD + pain on movement→Favours optic neuritis / anterior optic neuropathy, not papilloedema
Disc pallor with cupping→Chronic damage / glaucomatous or atrophic disc, not acute papilloedema
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY

The main pitfall is pseudopapilloedema — a disc that looks swollen but is not. Optic disc drusen (calcified deposits, often with a lumpy margin and no obscured vessels or haemorrhages), hypermetropic (small, crowded) discs and myelinated nerve fibres can all mimic true swelling; drusen may show autofluorescence and can be confirmed on B-scan ultrasound or OCT. Conversely, remember papilloedema is by definition bilateral, so unilateral swelling should prompt thought about local optic nerve pathology. Assessing the disc through an undilated pupil, poor patient fixation, and media opacities all limit the view. Do not be reassured by normal acuity, as it is often preserved until late.

🚩 Papilloedema signals raised ICP and mandates urgent neuroimaging (CT/MRI + venography) to exclude a mass lesion or venous sinus thrombosis. Never perform a lumbar puncture before imaging excludes a space-occupying lesion — LP in the presence of a mass and raised ICP risks fatal cerebral (tonsillar) herniation.
🎓 The earliest fundoscopic sign of raised ICP is loss of spontaneous venous pulsation. It is absent in up to ~10% of normal people, so its absence alone is not diagnostic, but a clearly present pulsation makes significantly raised ICP unlikely.

Optic atrophy is a fundoscopic sign, not a diagnosis: a pale, white optic disc caused by irreversible loss of retinal ganglion cell axons within the optic nerve. It is the final common endpoint of any process that damages the anterior visual pathway, and it reflects loss of the capillary network that normally gives the disc its healthy pink hue. Clinically it is accompanied by reduced visual acuity, dyschromatopsia (impaired colour vision, especially red desaturation), a visual field defect, and frequently a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) when the damage is unilateral or asymmetric. Recognising the sign is only half the task — the exam skill lies in working through the causes and distinguishing glaucomatous cupping from non-glaucomatous pallor.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

You look for optic atrophy whenever a patient presents with unexplained reduced acuity, a colour-vision complaint, or a visual field defect that localises to the optic nerve. The disc is normally pink because of a dense superficial capillary network overlying the neural rim. When axons die, these capillaries regress and the underlying white lamina cribrosa and glial tissue show through — hence pallor. Pallor takes 4–6 weeks to develop after an acute insult, so an acutely damaged nerve (e.g. recent optic neuritis) can look normal or swollen before it later turns pale.

🔬Pale disc
Loss of capillary pink; white/pale, well-defined margins
🎨Dyschromatopsia
Red desaturation; often the earliest functional clue
👁️RAPD
Present when damage is unilateral/asymmetric
📉Field defect
Central/centrocaecal scotoma or nerve-fibre pattern
2HOW IT IS ELICITED

Assessment combines function at the bedside with direct visualisation of the disc:

Acuity & colour: Snellen chart, then Ishihara plates — ask the patient to compare the redness of a red target between the two eyes to detect subtle red desaturation.
Swinging-light test: swing a bright light between the eyes; a dilating (rather than constricting) response on the affected side confirms an RAPD.
Fundoscopy: in a darkened room, ideally after dilating with tropicamide 1%, examine the disc colour, margins and cup. A normal disc is pink with a sharp margin and a physiological cup occupying roughly a third of its diameter.
Fields: confrontation at the bedside, formal automated perimetry to characterise the defect.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the fundoscopic appearance of a chalky-white, well-demarcated optic disc with a normal-sized cup (non-glaucomatous pallor), contrasted with a deeply excavated glaucomatous disc.
3INTERPRETATION — CAUSE CATEGORIES

Once atrophy is confirmed, the pattern of the disc plus the history points to a cause. Match the clue to the category:

Temporal pallor + young adult + prior painful vision loss→Previous optic neuritis / multiple sclerosis
Pallor WITH deep cupping (cup:disc ≥ 0.7) + raised IOP→Chronic glaucoma
Sudden painless loss + altitudinal field defect + vasculopath→Ischaemic optic neuropathy (consider GCA)
Slowly progressive loss + optic atrophy in one eye, swelling in the other→Compression (pituitary tumour, meningioma)
Bilateral, symmetrical, painless + poor diet / alcohol / drugs→Toxic / nutritional (B12 deficiency, methanol, ethambutol)
Young male + bilateral sequential central scotomas + family history→Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy

Mnemonic for causes — think: the classic categories are vascular, inflammatory, compressive, glaucomatous, toxic/nutritional and hereditary.

4GLAUCOMATOUS CUPPING vs NON-GLAUCOMATOUS PALLOR & PITFALLS

The single most important interpretive distinction is whether the disc is cupped or merely pale:

Glaucoma: cup enlarges FIRST, rim thins, cup:disc ≥ 0.7, bayoneting of vessels→Pathological CUPPING with relatively preserved rim colour
Non-glaucomatous: disc goes PALE with a normal-sized cup→PALLOR out of proportion to cupping — look for neuro cause

Key pitfalls and limitations to remember:

Pallor is a late sign — an acutely damaged nerve may look normal for weeks, so a pink disc does not exclude serious optic nerve disease.
A physiologically pale or small disc, or myelinated nerve fibres, can be over-called as atrophy in a well-seeing eye — correlate with function.
Never label atrophy as glaucoma just because the disc looks pale. Pallor greater than cupping, or in a patient under 50 with normal IOP, mandates neuro-imaging to exclude a compressive lesion.
🚩 Bilateral optic atrophy, or unexplained pallor exceeding cupping, must not be dismissed as glaucoma — it can signal a compressive lesion (e.g. pituitary tumour) or reversible toxic/nutritional cause (B12, methanol, ethambutol). Both demand urgent investigation (MRI, bloods, drug review) because early action can save the fellow eye.
🎓 Foster Kennedy syndrome = optic atrophy in one eye (from direct compression) with papilloedema in the other (from raised ICP), classically caused by a frontal lobe or olfactory groove meningioma — a high-yield eponym linking atrophy to compression.

A Roth spot is a retinal haemorrhage with a pale or white centre seen on fundoscopy. The surrounding red flame- or blot-shaped haemorrhage rings a central core of fibrin, platelet aggregate, or clustered inflammatory/white cells. It is best known as a sign of infective endocarditis, but it is thoroughly non-specific — the key message is that a Roth spot is a clue that prompts a search for a systemic cause, not a diagnosis in itself.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE — why it matters

Roth spots are usually found incidentally during fundoscopy in a patient being worked up for systemic illness (fever of unknown origin, new murmur, anaemia, bruising, or malaise). The white centre reflects the mechanism of the haemorrhage: capillary rupture in the nerve-fibre layer with a central plug of fibrin–platelet thrombus or a focal collection of leucocytes. Because several unrelated processes can produce this same appearance, the finding is a shared final pathway of retinal microvascular injury rather than a disease.

🦠Infective endocarditis
Classic association; immune-complex or septic microembolic origin
🩸Leukaemia
White centre = leukaemic cell aggregate; look for other retinal infiltrates
🫥Severe anaemia
Especially with thrombocytopenia; retinal haemorrhages common
🍬Diabetes
Diabetic retinopathy — microvascular leakage
💢Hypertension
Accelerated/malignant HTN with retinal haemorrhages
⛰️Hypoxia / altitude
High-altitude retinopathy; also HIV and connective-tissue disease
2HOW IT IS ELICITED — fundoscopy technique

Roth spots are seen on direct or indirect ophthalmoscopy, ideally after pupillary dilation with a short-acting mydriatic (e.g. tropicamide 1%) to widen the view of the mid-peripheral and posterior retina where they cluster.

Dim the room and ask the patient to fixate on a distant point; approach temporally at ~15° to find the optic disc, then track the vascular arcades outward.
A Roth spot appears as a flame- or blot-shaped red haemorrhage with a discrete white/pale centre, typically near the posterior pole along vessels.
A normal fundus shows a sharp pink disc, a cup:disc ratio around 0.3, and unbroken vessels with no haemorrhage, exudate, or pale-centred lesions.
Always examine both eyes and document number and location — bilateral scattered spots favour a systemic haematological or embolic cause.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the ophthalmic view / finding: fundoscopic view of a posterior-pole retinal haemorrhage with a pale white centre (Roth spot) lying along a vascular arcade.
3INTERPRETATION — what to do next

The finding should trigger a directed systemic work-up guided by the clinical picture. Match the association to the appropriate first-line investigation.

Fever + new/changed murmur→Suspect infective endocarditis — three sets of blood cultures + echocardiography (TTE, then TOE)
Fatigue, bruising, weight loss, lymphadenopathy→Suspect leukaemia — FBC with blood film, then haematology referral
Pallor, breathlessness, known blood loss→Severe anaemia ± thrombocytopenia — FBC, haematinics
Very high BP, headache, other hypertensive retinal changes→Accelerated hypertension — BP assessment and end-organ work-up
Known diabetes with dot/blot haemorrhages & exudates→Diabetic retinopathy — glycaemic review and retinal screening

Roth spots themselves rarely threaten vision unless they overlie the fovea; management is directed entirely at the underlying cause.

4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
Non-specific: a Roth spot never confirms endocarditis — it is present in only a minority of endocarditis cases and appears in many other conditions.
Easily missed: peripheral spots are hard to see through an undilated pupil or with an inexperienced examiner; a normal-looking central fundus does not exclude them.
Mimics: cotton-wool spots, hard exudates, and myelinated nerve fibres can be mistaken for the white centre — look for the surrounding rim of haemorrhage that defines a true Roth spot.
Anticoagulation/thrombocytopenia can produce pale-centred haemorrhages that are not embolic in origin.
🚩 A Roth spot is a sign, not a diagnosis — do NOT anchor on endocarditis and stop. In a febrile patient with a murmur it mandates urgent blood cultures and echocardiography, but an isolated finding in a well patient still requires an FBC to exclude leukaemia or severe anaemia. Failure to work up the underlying cause is the real danger.
🎓 High-yield: the classic triad taught for infective endocarditis eye/skin signs is Roth spots (retina), Janeway lesions (painless palms/soles) and Osler nodes (painful pulps) — but examiners love that Roth spots are NON-specific and also occur in leukaemia, anaemia, diabetes, hypertension and hypoxia.

Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings are golden-brown to greenish rings at the corneal periphery caused by copper deposition in Descemet's membrane. They are the classic slit-lamp sign of Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration), an autosomal-recessive defect of copper excretion. In the right clinical context, a young patient with liver disease and a movement disorder, KF rings strongly support a treatable inherited diagnosis, so they are actively sought whenever Wilson's is considered.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Wilson's disease results from mutations in the ATP7B copper-transporting ATPase. Copper cannot be incorporated into caeruloplasmin or excreted into bile, so it accumulates first in the liver, then spills into blood and deposits in the brain (basal ganglia), kidneys and the eye. In the cornea, copper precipitates in Descemet's membrane at the limbus, producing the visible ring. KF rings are therefore a clinical marker of systemic copper overload, not a primary eye disease.

🧬ATP7B defect
impaired biliary copper excretion & caeruloplasmin loading
🩸Low caeruloplasmin
serum caeruloplasmin typically reduced
💧High urinary copper
raised 24-hour urinary copper excretion
🧠Neuro / hepatic
tremor, dystonia, dysarthria, chronic liver disease
2HOW IT IS ELICITED

KF rings are examined on the slit-lamp biomicroscope. The patient is seated at the slit-lamp with chin and forehead steadied; a bright, narrow slit beam is directed at the peripheral cornea and the examiner inspects the deep corneal layers near the limbus. The ring appears as a curved band of pigment in Descemet's membrane, usually densest superiorly and inferiorly first, then becoming circumferential.

Colour ranges from golden-brown to green; it lies just inside the limbus.
Early/faint rings may be visible only on gonioscopy, which brings the peripheral angle and Descemet's membrane into direct view.
No dye or dilating drop is required to see the ring itself; slit-lamp illumination is sufficient.
A sunflower (chalcosis-like) cataract from lens copper may coexist and is also seen on slit-lamp.
📷 Image placeholder — slit-lamp view of a golden-brown Kayser-Fleischer ring at the peripheral cornea (limbus), densest superiorly and inferiorly.
3INTERPRETATION

KF rings are interpreted alongside the copper studies and clinical picture. They are near-universal in neurological Wilson's disease but may be absent in early or purely hepatic presentations, so their absence does not exclude the diagnosis.

KF rings + young patient with liver disease + tremor→strongly supports Wilson's disease; confirm with copper studies
Low serum caeruloplasmin + high 24-hour urinary copper→biochemical corroboration of copper overload
KF rings in a patient with neuropsychiatric signs→virtually always present with neurological Wilson's
Rings regress on treatment (chelation / zinc)→useful marker of response to de-coppering therapy
Sunflower cataract also present→further evidence of ocular copper deposition in Wilson's
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY

KF rings are highly suggestive but must be confirmed. Naked-eye or torch examination is unreliable for faint rings, and diffuse corneal arcus in older patients can be mistaken for them, though arcus has a clear zone between it and the limbus whereas KF pigment reaches the limbus.

Absent rings do not exclude Wilson's, especially in children and hepatic-only disease.
Rare copper-overload states (e.g. chronic cholestatic liver disease) can occasionally produce similar rings.
A formal slit-lamp examination by an ophthalmologist is required; do not rely on bedside inspection to confirm or refute the sign.
🚩 Wilson's disease is treatable but progressive and can be fatal if missed. Do not dismiss KF rings as a benign eye finding, refer urgently for copper studies and specialist (hepatology/neurology) assessment, as early chelation prevents irreversible neurological and hepatic damage.
🎓 KF rings are pathognomonic of copper deposition, not of the eye itself: think Wilson's disease in any patient under 40 with unexplained liver disease, a movement disorder or psychiatric change, and always request a slit-lamp examination plus serum caeruloplasmin and 24-hour urinary copper.

Phenylephrine blanching is a simple bedside test used to distinguish episcleritis (a benign, superficial inflammation of the episclera) from scleritis (a serious, deep inflammation of the sclera) in a patient presenting with a red, injected eye. A drop of topical phenylephrine 2.5% (a sympathomimetic vasoconstrictor) is instilled: it constricts the superficial episcleral vascular plexus but not the deep scleral vessels. If the redness fades (blanches) the injection is superficial and points to episcleritis; if it persists, the deeper scleral vessels are involved and scleritis must be assumed until proven otherwise.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used when a patient has a segmental or diffuse red eye and you must separate a self-limiting condition from a sight-threatening one. The conjunctiva and episclera share a superficial vascular network that responds to topical vasoconstrictors; the deep scleral vessels (and their overlying deep episcleral plexus) do not.

🔬Superficial plexus
Episcleral vessels that CONSTRICT with phenylephrine → blanching in episcleritis
🩸Deep plexus
Scleral vessels that do NOT constrict → persistent redness in scleritis
💊Phenylephrine 2.5%
α-agonist vasoconstrictor; the low 2.5% strength is used, not 10%
🎯Purpose
Depth of injection = the pivotal discriminator between the two diagnoses
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Examine and photograph/document the red eye first, noting the pattern and depth of injection at the slit lamp.
Instil one drop of topical phenylephrine 2.5% onto the affected area (a topical anaesthetic may be given first for comfort).
Wait approximately 10–15 minutes for the vasoconstrictor to take effect.
Re-examine the same area and compare the degree of redness with the baseline appearance.

A helpful adjunct: episcleral vessels are more superficial and can be moved gently over the sclera with a cotton bud, whereas scleral vessels are fixed and deeper.

3INTERPRETATION
Redness BLANCHES (fades)→Superficial injection = EPISCLERITIS; benign, self-limiting
Redness DOES NOT blanch→Deep injection = SCLERITIS; sight-threatening emergency
Eye not tender, mild irritation only→Favours episcleritis
Severe boring pain, worse at night, wakes patient, globe tender to palpation→Favours scleritis
Bluish/violaceous hue to the sclera→Scleral thinning – deep scleral involvement
Associated RA, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, or other systemic vasculitis→Strongly suggests scleritis; needs systemic work-up
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
The test is supportive, not definitive – pain severity, tenderness and systemic associations must be weighed together.
Partial or equivocal blanching in mixed or necrotising disease should be treated as scleritis (the more dangerous diagnosis) until specialist review.
Do not use 10% phenylephrine indiscriminately; the higher concentration carries a systemic hypertensive risk, and 2.5% is sufficient for this test.
Never let a normal-looking eye reassure you if the patient reports deep, boring pain – posterior scleritis can present with minimal visible redness.
🚩 Scleritis is a sight-threatening ocular emergency. Failure to blanch, severe pain and globe tenderness mandate SAME-DAY ophthalmology referral. It is frequently associated with systemic vasculitis (e.g. RA, granulomatosis with polyangiitis) and requires systemic anti-inflammatory / immunosuppressive treatment (oral NSAIDs, systemic steroids, or steroid-sparing agents) – topical drops alone are inadequate.
🎓 Exam pearl: the classic triad separating the two is BLANCHING + no tenderness + trivial pain = episcleritis, versus NO blanching + globe tenderness + severe boring pain that wakes the patient = scleritis. If a red eye is exquisitely painful and does not blanch, think scleritis and screen for underlying systemic disease.
